# Australian Culture: full content

Everything in the guide at https://australianculture.biblioverse.org/ as plain Markdown, stop by stop, with a link to each page and to the matching Wikipedia article. Content updated November 2026.

## Famous Aussies

https://australianculture.biblioverse.org/famous-aussies.html


### Famous worldwide

- **Nicole Kidman**: (Film and TV) Won the Oscar for The Hours (2002). From Moulin Rouge! to Big Little Lies, she’s one of the most awarded actors of her generation. Grew up in Sydney. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicole_Kidman>
- **Hugh Jackman**: (Film and TV) Played Wolverine in X-Men for 17 years and starred in musicals like The Greatest Showman and Les Misérables. Born in Sydney. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Jackman>
- **Margot Robbie**: (Film and TV) Went from Neighbours to The Wolf of Wall Street, Harley Quinn and Barbie (2023), which she also produced through LuckyChap. Born in Dalby, Queensland, and raised on the Gold Coast. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margot_Robbie>
- **Chris Hemsworth**: (Film and TV) Marvel’s Thor and the most followed Australian actor. Got his start on Home and Away. Brothers Liam and Luke act too. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Hemsworth>
- **Cate Blanchett**: (Film and TV) Two Oscars, for The Aviator and Blue Jasmine, and Galadriel in The Lord of the Rings. Born in Melbourne. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cate_Blanchett>
- **Heath Ledger**: (Film and TV) Born in Perth, he won a posthumous Oscar as the Joker in The Dark Knight (2008). Also unforgettable in Brokeback Mountain. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heath_Ledger>
- **Russell Crowe**: (Film and TV) Born in New Zealand and raised in Sydney, he won the Oscar for Gladiator (2000). He even co-owns a rugby league club, the South Sydney Rabbitohs. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Crowe>
- **Geoffrey Rush**: (Film and TV) Oscar for Shine (1996) and Barbossa in Pirates of the Caribbean. One of the few actors with the “triple crown”: an Oscar, an Emmy and a Tony. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_Rush>
- **Naomi Watts**: (Film and TV) Born in England and raised in Sydney. Broke through in Mulholland Drive and was Oscar-nominated for 21 Grams and The Impossible. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naomi_Watts>
- **Hugo Weaving**: (Film and TV) Agent Smith in The Matrix, Elrond in The Lord of the Rings and one of the drag queens in The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugo_Weaving>
- **Toni Collette**: (Film and TV) Oscar-nominated for The Sixth Sense. Made her name in Muriel’s Wedding (1994) and shone again in the horror film Hereditary. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toni_Collette>
- **Jacob Elordi**: (Film and TV) From Brisbane to the world: Euphoria, The Kissing Booth, Saltburn and Elvis in Priscilla. Played the creature in Guillermo del Toro’s Frankenstein (2025). <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Elordi>
- **Rebel Wilson**: (Film and TV) Fat Amy in Pitch Perfect. Started out in Aussie TV comedy, in shows like Pizza. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebel_Wilson>
- **Eric Bana**: (Film and TV) Went from sketch comedy (Full Frontal) to Hulk, Troy and Munich. His first big role was the criminal Chopper (2000). <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Bana>
- **Rose Byrne**: (Film and TV) Comedies like Bridesmaids and Neighbors, the horror Insidious and the series Physical. Born in Sydney. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rose_Byrne>
- **Guy Pearce**: (Film and TV) Discovered on Neighbours, then L.A. Confidential, Memento and Priscilla. Oscar-nominated for The Brutalist (2024). <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guy_Pearce>
- **Mel Gibson**: (Film and TV) Born in the US and raised in Sydney, he became famous as Mad Max (1979) and won the Best Director Oscar for Braveheart. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel_Gibson>
- **Paul Hogan**: (Film and TV) Crocodile Dundee (1986), the film that introduced the “Aussie” to the world with “That’s not a knife. That’s a knife.” <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Hogan>
- **Isla Fisher**: (Film and TV) Born in Oman and raised in Perth. Comedies like Wedding Crashers and Confessions of a Shopaholic; she also writes children’s books. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isla_Fisher>
- **Elizabeth Debicki**: (Film and TV) Princess Diana in The Crown (Golden Globe in 2024), and also in Tenet and The Great Gatsby. Grew up in Melbourne. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Debicki>
- **Steve Irwin**: (Film and TV) “Crikey!” The Crocodile Hunter brought Australian wildlife to TV screens around the world. He died in 2006; his kids Bindi and Robert carry on at Australia Zoo. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Irwin>
- **Errol Flynn**: (Film and TV) Classic Hollywood’s swashbuckling heart-throb, star of Captain Blood and The Adventures of Robin Hood (1938). Born in Hobart, Tasmania. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Errol_Flynn>
- **Baz Luhrmann**: (Film and TV) Director of Romeo + Juliet, Moulin Rouge!, The Great Gatsby and Elvis. Over the top, musical and bursting with colour. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baz_Luhrmann>
- **George Miller**: (Film and TV) Creator of Mad Max (from 1979 to Furiosa in 2024). He also made Babe and won the Best Animated Feature Oscar for Happy Feet. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Miller_(filmmaker)>
- **Elle Macpherson**: (Models) “The Body”. Supermodel of the 80s and 90s and record holder for Sports Illustrated Swimsuit covers. Born in Sydney. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elle_Macpherson>
- **Miranda Kerr**: (Models) The first Australian Victoria’s Secret Angel. Founded the organic skincare brand Kora Organics. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miranda_Kerr>
- **Catriona Gray**: (Models) Born in Cairns to a Scottish-Australian dad and a Filipino mum. Won Miss Universe 2018 representing the Philippines. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catriona_Gray>
- **Gemma Ward**: (Models) Discovered at 14 in Perth, she became one of the most sought-after faces in fashion in the 2000s (Prada, Chanel, Vogue). <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gemma_Ward>
- **Abbey Lee**: (Models) Melbourne supermodel turned actor: one of Immortan Joe’s wives in Mad Max: Fury Road. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbey_Lee>
- **Adut Akech**: (Models) Born in South Sudan and raised in Adelaide after arriving as a refugee. Model of the Year at the British Fashion Awards in 2019. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adut_Akech>
- **Jordan Barrett**: (Models) From Byron Bay, one of the world’s best-known male models, with campaigns for Versace and Tom Ford. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_Barrett>
- **Shanina Shaik**: (Models) Born in Melbourne, she walked for Victoria’s Secret and first got noticed on Australia’s Next Top Model. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanina_Shaik>
- **Duckie Thot**: (Models) Daughter of South Sudanese parents, raised in Melbourne. Found fame on Australia’s Next Top Model and became a face of Fenty Beauty. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duckie_Thot>
- **Robyn Lawley**: (Models) A plus-size pioneer: the first curve model on the cover of Vogue Italia and in Sports Illustrated Swimsuit. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robyn_Lawley>
- **Kayla Itsines**: (Content creators) Adelaide personal trainer who created the Bikini Body Guide and the Sweat app, and became one of the biggest fitness influencers on the planet. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kayla_Itsines>
- **Tammy Hembrow**: (Content creators) Gold Coast fitness influencer behind the Saski Collection clothing label and the Tammy Fit app.
- **Supercar Blondie**: (Content creators) Alex Hirschi, from Brisbane, shows off luxury cars and tech. One of the biggest motoring creators in the world. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Hirschi>
- **Celeste Barber**: (Content creators) Comedian who recreates celebrity and model photos, “real life” style. In 2020 she raised more than A$50 million for bushfire relief. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celeste_Barber>
- **Ben & Zara Tate**: (Content creators) A couple making comedy sketches about relationships, with millions of followers on Instagram and TikTok.
- **Vinh Giang**: (Content creators) Melbourne magician and communication coach whose videos on how to speak well go viral worldwide.
- **How Ridiculous**: (Content creators) Perth trio famous for impossible trick shots from crazy heights, with Guinness records and billions of YouTube views. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/How_Ridiculous>
- **Aunty Donna**: (Content creators) Absurdist Melbourne comedy troupe that went from YouTube to their own Netflix series (Aunty Donna’s Big Ol’ House of Fun). <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunty_Donna>
- **Lachlan**: (Content creators) Lachlan Power, Fortnite and Minecraft gamer with more than 15 million subscribers. Founded the PWR group and its clothing brand. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lachlan_Power>
- **Loserfruit**: (Content creators) Kathleen Belsten, from Melbourne, one of the first women to get her own skin in Fortnite. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loserfruit>
- **Robert Irwin**: (Content creators) Steve Irwin’s son, a wildlife photographer and Australia Zoo presenter. Won the US Dancing with the Stars in 2025. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Irwin>
- **Patrick White**: (Literature and ideas) The only Australian to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1973. Author of Voss and The Tree of Man, dense portraits of the country’s people and landscape. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White>
- **Thomas Keneally**: (Literature and ideas) Wrote Schindler’s Ark, winner of the 1982 Booker Prize, which became Spielberg’s Schindler’s List and won seven Oscars. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Keneally>
- **Peter Carey**: (Literature and ideas) One of only a handful of writers to win the Booker Prize twice: for Oscar and Lucinda (1988) and True History of the Kelly Gang (2001). <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Carey_(novelist)>
- **Markus Zusak**: (Literature and ideas) Sydney author of The Book Thief (2005), a worldwide bestseller that became a film in 2013. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markus_Zusak>
- **Colleen McCullough**: (Literature and ideas) A neurophysiologist turned novelist who wrote The Thorn Birds (1977), one of the best-selling Australian books ever and a hit TV miniseries in the 80s. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colleen_McCullough>
- **Peter Singer**: (Literature and ideas) Moral philosopher born in Melbourne, one of the most influential thinkers alive. Animal Liberation (1975) launched the animal rights movement, and his ideas inspired effective altruism. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer>
- **David Chalmers**: (Literature and ideas) Philosopher and cognitive scientist who coined the “hard problem of consciousness”: why do we have inner experience at all? Professor at NYU, he also popularised the famous philosophical zombies. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Chalmers>

### Famous in Australia

- **Ray Martin**: (TV and radio) Journalist and presenter of 60 Minutes, Midday and A Current Affair. He won the Gold Logie, Australian TV’s top award, five times. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Martin_(television_presenter)>
- **Bert Newton**: (TV and radio) “Mr Television”: more than 60 years on air, from In Melbourne Tonight to Good Morning Australia, and four Gold Logies. He died in 2021. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bert_Newton>
- **Karl Stefanovic**: (TV and radio) Co-host of Nine’s Today breakfast show from 2005 to 2018 and again since 2020. He won the Gold Logie in 2011. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Stefanovic>
- **Lisa Wilkinson**: (TV and radio) Became editor of Dolly magazine at 21, then co-hosted Today and The Project. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisa_Wilkinson>
- **Leigh Sales**: (TV and radio) ABC journalist who hosted 7.30 from 2011 to 2022, known for tough interviews with politicians. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leigh_Sales>
- **Grant Denyer**: (TV and radio) Host of Family Feud, former Sunrise weatherman and racing driver. He won the Gold Logie in 2018. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grant_Denyer>
- **Sonia Kruger**: (TV and radio) Former dancer turned one of the country’s best-known hosts, fronting The Voice and Big Brother. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonia_Kruger>
- **Andrew Denton**: (TV and radio) Interviewer on the ABC’s Enough Rope and creator of comedy shows. Now a leading voice for voluntary assisted dying. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Denton>
- **Molly Meldrum**: (TV and radio) The man in the cowboy hat on Countdown (1974–1987), the show that helped launch acts like AC/DC and Skyhooks. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molly_Meldrum>
- **Costa Georgiadis**: (TV and radio) The bearded gardener of the ABC’s Gardening Australia, who makes everyone want to start a veggie patch. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Georgiadis>
- **Magda Szubanski**: (Film and TV) Sharon in Kath & Kim and Esme in Babe. She was one of the faces of the 2017 marriage equality campaign. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magda_Szubanski>
- **Deborah Mailman**: (Film and TV) Bidjara actor from The Sapphires, Offspring and Mystery Road. The first Aboriginal woman to win the AFI award for best actress, in 1998. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deborah_Mailman>
- **Ernie Dingo**: (Film and TV) Yamatji actor and presenter, the face of travel show The Great Outdoors and films like Crocodile Dundee II. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernie_Dingo>
- **Cathy Freeman**: (Sport) Lit the cauldron and won the 400 m at the Sydney 2000 Olympics, one of the most moving moments in the nation’s history. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathy_Freeman>
- **Don Bradman**: (Sport) The greatest cricketer of all time, with a Test batting average of 99.94. Every Aussie knows that number. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Bradman>
- **Dawn Fraser**: (Sport) Swimmer who won the 100 m freestyle at three Olympics in a row (1956, 1960 and 1964). <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawn_Fraser>
- **Johnathan Thurston**: (Sport) Indigenous rugby league great and North Queensland Cowboys hero, who won them the 2015 premiership with a field goal in golden point. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnathan_Thurston>
- **Jennifer Hawkins**: (Fashion and music) Miss Universe 2004, then a TV host and one of the best-known faces in Australian fashion and advertising. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer_Hawkins>
- **Megan Gale**: (Fashion and music) Perth model who became a star in Italy and was, for years, the face of David Jones at home. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Gale>
- **Jessica Origliasso**: (Fashion and music) Brisbane singer, songwriter and producer, born in 1984. With her identical twin Lisa, she makes up The Veronicas. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessica_Origliasso>
- **Lisa Origliasso**: (Fashion and music) Singer and songwriter raised in Albany Creek, Queensland. Jessica’s identical twin and the other half of The Veronicas. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisa_Origliasso>
- **Karl Kruszelnicki**: (Science and culture) Dr Karl, the country’s best-known science communicator. He has answered listeners’ questions on radio for decades, written dozens of books and won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2002 for research into belly-button lint. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Kruszelnicki>
- **Ita Buttrose**: (Science and culture) Founding editor of Cleo, editor of The Women’s Weekly and ABC chair from 2019 to 2024. Australian of the Year in 2013. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ita_Buttrose>

## Music

https://australianculture.biblioverse.org/music.html


### Artists and bands

- **AC/DC**: (Rock · 1973) Brothers Malcolm and Angus Young (in his school uniform) built one of the biggest rock bands in history. Back in Black is one of the best-selling albums of all time. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AC%2FDC>
- **INXS**: (Rock · 1977) Michael Hutchence and co. took Aussie rock to the top in the 80s with Need You Tonight and Never Tear Us Apart. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/INXS>
- **Midnight Oil**: (Rock · 1972) Political rock from Sydney. Beds Are Burning (1987) is about handing land back to Aboriginal people. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnight_Oil>
- **Men at Work**: (Rock · 1978) Down Under (1981), the country’s unofficial anthem: “Do you come from a land down under?” It went to No. 1 in the US and the UK. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Men_at_Work>
- **Cold Chisel**: (Rock · 1973) The sound of the Aussie pub. Khe Sanh and Flame Trees still get sung in chorus. Frontman Jimmy Barnes has a huge solo career too. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_Chisel>
- **Crowded House**: (Rock · 1985) Melbourne band led by New Zealander Neil Finn. Don’t Dream It’s Over became a worldwide classic. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crowded_House>
- **The Easybeats**: (Rock · 1964) A Sydney band of young migrants. Friday on My Mind (1966) was the first Aussie rock song to become a worldwide hit. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Easybeats>
- **Little River Band**: (Rock · 1975) Melbourne soft rock that landed Reminiscing and Lonesome Loser on American radio. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_River_Band>
- **Icehouse**: (Rock · 1977) Sydney new wave. Great Southern Land (1982) is practically a musical portrait of the country. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icehouse_(band)>
- **The Saints**: (Rock · 1973) Brisbane band whose (I’m) Stranded (1976) is one of the first punk records anywhere. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Saints_(Australian_band)>
- **Hunters & Collectors**: (Rock · 1981) From Melbourne. Holy Grail became an AFL Grand Final anthem, and Throw Your Arms Around Me gets sung at every wedding. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunters_%26_Collectors>
- **Divinyls**: (Rock · 1980) Fronted by Chrissy Amphlett in a school uniform. I Touch Myself (1990) was a hit around the world. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divinyls>
- **Hoodoo Gurus**: (Rock · 1981) Sydney garage rock with huge hooks, like What’s My Scene? (1987). <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoodoo_Gurus>
- **The Living End**: (Rock · 1994) Melbourne punk and rockabilly trio with a double bass. Prisoner of Society is a 90s classic. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Living_End>
- **Spiderbait**: (Rock · 1991) From country NSW. Their version of Black Betty (2004) went to No. 1 in Australia. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiderbait>
- **Jet**: (Rock · 2001) Melbourne band that went global with Are You Gonna Be My Girl (2003), helped along by an iPod ad. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_(band)>
- **Wolfmother**: (Rock · 2004) Seventies-flavoured hard rock from Sydney. Won the 2007 Grammy for Best Hard Rock Performance with Woman. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfmother>
- **Gang of Youths**: (Rock · 2012) Big-hearted Sydney rock. Go Farther in Lightness (2017) won the ARIA for Album of the Year. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gang_of_Youths>
- **Amyl and the Sniffers**: (Rock · 2016) Melbourne punk fronted by Amy Taylor. Won the ARIA for Best Rock Album in 2019. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amyl_and_the_Sniffers>
- **Bee Gees**: (Pop · 1958) The Gibb brothers were born on the Isle of Man but started their career in Brisbane. From Stayin’ Alive to How Deep Is Your Love, they defined the disco era. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bee_Gees>
- **Kylie Minogue**: (Pop · 1987) The “princess of pop”. Went from Neighbours to hits like Can’t Get You Out of My Head and Padam Padam (a Grammy in 2024). <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kylie_Minogue>
- **Olivia Newton-John**: (Pop · 1966) Born in England and raised in Melbourne. Sandy in Grease (1978) and the voice of Physical and Xanadu. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olivia_Newton-John>
- **Savage Garden**: (Pop · 1993) Brisbane duo behind the big ballads Truly Madly Deeply and I Knew I Loved You, which topped the charts in the US and around the world. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savage_Garden>
- **The Veronicas**: (Pop · 2005) Pop rock duo of Brisbane twins Jessica and Lisa Origliasso. Their debut album, The Secret Life Of... (2005), went to number two in Australia on the back of the hit 4ever. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Veronicas>
- **Natalie Imbruglia**: (Pop · 1997) Another Neighbours actor turned singer: Torn (1997) was one of the biggest hits of the 90s. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natalie_Imbruglia>
- **John Farnham**: (Pop · 1967) You’re the Voice (1986) is practically a second national anthem. “The Voice” is one of the country’s most loved singers. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Farnham>
- **Sia**: (Pop · 1997) Adelaide singer-songwriter behind Chandelier and Cheap Thrills. She’s also written hits for Rihanna, Beyoncé and Britney. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sia>
- **Silverchair**: (Rock · 1992) Newcastle teenagers who blew up in the grunge era with Tomorrow (1994). Daniel Johns was just 15. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silverchair>
- **Powderfinger**: (Rock · 1989) The Brisbane band that ruled Aussie alternative rock through the 90s and 2000s, with My Happiness. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Powderfinger>
- **Tame Impala**: (Indie · 2007) Kevin Parker’s psychedelic project from Perth. Currents (2015) became a touchstone; The Less I Know the Better is an indie anthem. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tame_Impala>
- **Gotye**: (Indie · 2003) Somebody That I Used to Know (2011), with Kimbra, won two Grammys and had one of the most watched music videos of the decade. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gotye>
- **5 Seconds of Summer**: (Pop · 2011) Sydney pop-punk band that broke through supporting One Direction. Youngblood (2018) spent 8 weeks at No. 1 in Australia. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5_Seconds_of_Summer>
- **Troye Sivan**: (Pop · 2013) Started on YouTube in Perth and became a pop icon with Youth and Rush (2023). <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troye_Sivan>
- **The Kid LAROI**: (Hip-hop · 2018) From Sydney, he made Stay (2021) with Justin Bieber, which spent 7 weeks at No. 1 in the US. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Kid_Laroi>
- **Tones and I**: (Pop · 2019) Was busking in Byron Bay when she released Dance Monkey, which spent a record 24 straight weeks at No. 1 in Australia. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tones_and_I>
- **Vance Joy**: (Indie · 2013) Riptide (2013) and its ukulele stayed in the charts for years and turn up at every singalong. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vance_Joy>
- **Flume**: (Electronic · 2011) Sydney producer who won the Grammy for Best Dance/Electronic Album in 2017 with Skin. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flume_(musician)>
- **RÜFÜS DU SOL**: (Electronic · 2010) Sydney trio making moody house music, with massive shows around the world. Innerbloom is a classic. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%BCf%C3%BCs_Du_Sol>
- **Empire of the Sun**: (Electronic · 2007) Synth-pop duo with theatrical costumes. Walking on a Dream (2008) was a global hit. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_of_the_Sun_(band)>
- **Hilltop Hoods**: (Hip-hop · 1994) The Adelaide crew that took Aussie hip-hop mainstream, with Cosby Sweater and Nosebleed Section. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilltop_Hoods>
- **Yothu Yindi**: (Indigenous · 1986) Arnhem Land band that blended rock with Yolŋu music. Treaty (1991) was the first song in an Aboriginal language to become a national hit. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yothu_Yindi>
- **Gurrumul**: (Indigenous · 2008) Geoffrey Gurrumul Yunupingu, a blind singer from Elcho Island, sang in Yolŋu. His debut album went triple platinum. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_Gurrumul_Yunupingu>
- **Paul Kelly**: (Folk · 1974) The country’s great storyteller in song. How to Make Gravy has become an Aussie Christmas tradition. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kelly_(Australian_musician)>
- **Nick Cave & The Bad Seeds**: (Rock · 1983) Gothic, literary rock from Melbourne. Red Right Hand is the theme of Peaky Blinders. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave_and_the_Bad_Seeds>
- **King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard**: (Rock · 2010) Melbourne band that releases albums at a ridiculous pace (more than 25), from psychedelia to thrash metal to jazz. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Gizzard_%26_the_Lizard_Wizard>
- **Rosé**: (Pop · 2016) Born in New Zealand and raised in Melbourne, the BLACKPINK singer released APT. (2024) with Bruno Mars, a global phenomenon. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ros%C3%A9_(singer)>
- **The Wiggles**: (Kids · 1991) The kids’ group in coloured skivvies is one of the country’s most lucrative cultural exports. Hot Potato! <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wiggles>

Sources: [Australia Para Todos: the history of Australian rock](https://australiaparatodos.wordpress.com/2026/07/20/a-historia-do-rock-australiano-e-os-artistas-australianos-de-rock-mais-populares)

## Film and TV

https://australianculture.biblioverse.org/film-and-tv.html


### Made in Australia

- **Mad Max**: (Aussie film · 1979) George Miller’s desert dystopia that launched Mel Gibson. The saga came roaring back with Fury Road (2015, 6 Oscars) and Furiosa (2024). <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mad_Max>
- **Crocodile Dundee**: (Aussie film · 1986) Paul Hogan as the outback bushman let loose in New York. Still one of the most successful Australian films ever. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crocodile_Dundee>
- **The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert**: (Aussie film · 1994) Three drag queens cross the outback in a bus. Won the Oscar for costume design and became a hit musical. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Adventures_of_Priscilla,_Queen_of_the_Desert>
- **Muriel’s Wedding**: (Aussie film · 1994) Toni Collette and a lot of ABBA in a cult comedy about a small-town girl. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muriel%27s_Wedding>
- **The Castle**: (Aussie film · 1997) The Kerrigans fight to keep their home next to the airport. Barely seen overseas, but every Australian can quote it: “Tell him he’s dreamin’.” <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Castle_(1997_Australian_film)>
- **Babe**: (Aussie film · 1995) Produced by George Miller and shot in NSW. Nominated for 7 Oscars and won for visual effects. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babe_(film)>
- **Moulin Rouge!**: (Aussie film · 2001) Baz Luhrmann’s musical with Nicole Kidman, shot at Fox Studios in Sydney. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moulin_Rouge!>
- **Happy Feet**: (Animation · 2006) A tap-dancing penguin animated by Sydney studio Animal Logic. Won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happy_Feet>
- **Elvis**: (Aussie film · 2022) Baz Luhrmann again, shot on the Gold Coast. Eight Oscar nominations. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvis_(2022_film)>
- **Picnic at Hanging Rock**: (Aussie film · 1975) The mystery of schoolgirls who vanish on an outing in 1900. Peter Weir and the Australian New Wave. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picnic_at_Hanging_Rock_(film)>
- **Gallipoli**: (Aussie film · 1981) Mel Gibson in the 1915 battle that shaped the national identity. Essential for understanding Anzac Day. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallipoli_(1981_film)>
- **Rabbit-Proof Fence**: (Aussie film · 2002) Three Aboriginal girls escape a settlement and walk 2,400 km home along a fence. A true story of the Stolen Generations. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabbit-Proof_Fence>
- **Lion**: (Aussie film · 2016) A boy from India adopted in Tasmania searches for his family using Google Earth. With Dev Patel and Nicole Kidman. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lion_(2016_film)>
- **Talk to Me**: (Aussie film · 2022) Horror from Adelaide’s Philippou brothers, the former RackaRacka YouTubers. A worldwide hit for A24. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talk_to_Me_(2022_film)>
- **The Babadook**: (Aussie film · 2014) Psychological horror from Adelaide’s Jennifer Kent. The monster even became an unlikely LGBTQ+ icon online. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Babadook>
- **Bluey**: (Animation · 2018) Brisbane-made cartoon about a family of blue heelers. One of the most watched kids’ shows in the world, a hit on Disney+ and the most watched children’s program on Australian TV, loved just as much by the parents. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bluey_(TV_series)>
- **Mary and Max**: (Animation · 2009) Adam Elliot’s claymation about a pen-pal friendship between a Melbourne girl and a man in New York. Opened the Sundance Film Festival. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_and_Max>
- **Harvie Krumpet**: (Animation · 2003) Adam Elliot’s claymation short, narrated by Geoffrey Rush, which won the Oscar for Best Animated Short. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvie_Krumpet>
- **Memoir of a Snail**: (Animation · 2024) Adam Elliot’s third stop-motion feature, about a woman who collects snails. Oscar-nominated for Best Animated Feature in 2025. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memoir_of_a_Snail>
- **The Lego Movie**: (Animation · 2014) All the animation was done by Sydney’s Animal Logic, the studio that also made Legend of the Guardians (2010) and Peter Rabbit (2018). <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Lego_Movie>
- **Dot and the Kangaroo**: (Animation · 1977) A girl lost in the bush is taken in by a kangaroo. A classic from Yoram Gross’s studio, mixing drawings with filmed landscapes. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dot_and_the_Kangaroo_(film)>
- **Blinky Bill**: (Animation · 1993) The cheeky koala from Dorothy Wall’s books (1933) became a TV cartoon and, in 2015, a CGI film. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blinky_Bill>
- **The Magic Pudding**: (Animation · 2000) Adapted from Norman Lindsay’s 1918 children’s book about a talking pudding that never runs out. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magic_Pudding_(film)>
- **FernGully: The Last Rainforest**: (Animation · 1992) An Australian–US co-production about fairies defending the rainforest. A 90s cult favourite. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FernGully:_The_Last_Rainforest>
- **Little J & Big Cuz**: (Animation · 2017) Kids’ cartoon about two Aboriginal cousins, in English and Indigenous languages. Made to help children understand Aboriginal culture. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_J_%26_Big_Cuz>
- **Kangaroo Beach**: (Animation · 2020) Young native animals train as lifeguards on an Aussie beach. Teaches water safety. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kangaroo_Beach>
- **100% Wolf**: (Animation · 2020) Sydney-made film about a werewolf who turns into a poodle. It became a series too. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/100%25_Wolf>
- **Kath & Kim**: (Aussie series · 2002) Comedy about a vain suburban mother and daughter. Catchphrases like “look at moiye” entered the language. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kath_%26_Kim>
- **Summer Heights High**: (Aussie series · 2007) Chris Lilley plays several characters at a high school. A huge cult hit (and looked at more critically today). <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Heights_High>
- **H2O: Just Add Water**: (Aussie series · 2006) Three Gold Coast teenagers become mermaids. A massive hit with kids around the world. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H2O:_Just_Add_Water>
- **Heartbreak High**: (Aussie series · 2022) Netflix reboot of the 90s series about a Sydney high school. Won an International Emmy in 2023. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heartbreak_High>
- **Wentworth**: (Aussie series · 2013) Women’s prison drama, a reimagining of the 70s series Prisoner (Cell Block H). <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wentworth_(TV_series)>
- **Mystery Road**: (Aussie series · 2018) Outback crime drama with an Aboriginal detective. One of the country’s best crime series. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mystery_Road_(TV_series)>
- **Deadloch**: (Aussie series · 2023) Prime Video crime comedy set in a small Tasmanian town, where two detectives who can’t stand each other investigate the bodies turning up on the beach. Created by Kate McCartney and Kate McLennan. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deadloch>
- **Last Stop Larrimah**: (Aussie series · 2023) HBO documentary about the disappearance of Paddy Moriarty in Larrimah, an outback town in the Northern Territory with about ten residents, where everyone is a suspect. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Stop_Larrimah>
- **Round the Twist**: (Kids’ series · 1989) The Twist family live in a lighthouse where Paul Jennings’ weird and wonderful stories come true. Shot at Split Point Lighthouse in Aireys Inlet, Victoria, with a theme every 90s kid can sing: “Have you ever...”. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round_the_Twist>
- **Johnson and Friends**: (Kids’ series · 1990) When the boy falls asleep, his toys come to life: Johnson the elephant and his mates have adventures in the bedroom. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_and_Friends>
- **Bananas in Pyjamas**: (Kids’ series · 1992) B1 and B2, two bananas in striped pyjamas, became one of the ABC’s biggest kids’ hits and sold to dozens of countries. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bananas_in_Pyjamas>
- **The Ferals**: (Kids’ series · 1994) ABC series with puppets of feral animals living secretly in a family home and causing chaos, with very Aussie humour. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ferals>
- **Ocean Girl**: (Kids’ series · 1994) A mysterious girl lives alone on an island and talks to a humpback whale. Kids’ sci-fi that screened in dozens of countries. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocean_Girl>
- **Spellbinder**: (Kids’ series · 1995) A Sydney teenager crosses into a parallel world. An Australian–Polish co-production that became a cult hit. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spellbinder_(TV_series)>
- **The Kangaroo Creek Gang**: (Kids’ series · 2002) Cartoon from Yoram Gross’s studio (the team behind Dot and the Kangaroo) about a gang of bush animals on adventures to protect their home. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kangaroo_Creek_Gang>
- **Bambaloo**: (Kids’ series · 2003) Seven’s preschool show with puppets and presenters, part of every early morning for kids growing up in the 2000s. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bambaloo>
- **Blue Water High**: (Kids’ series · 2005) Teenagers compete for a spot at a surf academy on Sydney’s northern beaches. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Water_High>
- **Mortified**: (Kids’ series · 2006) Eleven-year-old Taylor Fry is mortified by her family and escapes into a fantasy world in her own head. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortified>
- **Lockie Leonard**: (Kids’ series · 2007) A 12-year-old surfer moves to a small town in Western Australia. Based on Tim Winton’s books. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockie_Leonard_(TV_series)>
- **Dance Academy**: (Kids’ series · 2010) Ballet students fight for a place at the national dance academy in Sydney. It got a film in 2017. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dance_Academy>
- **Mako Mermaids**: (Kids’ series · 2013) A spin-off of H2O, with mermaids guarding Mako Island. A worldwide hit on Netflix. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mako:_Island_of_Secrets>
- **The New Adventures of Blinky Bill**: (Kids’ series · 1984) ABC series (1984–1987) where actors shared the screen with puppets of the cheeky koala and his bush mates. It stayed on air in repeats until 1991. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_Adventures_of_Blinky_Bill>

### What Australians watch

- **Neighbours**: (Soaps · 1985) The soap set on Ramsay Street in Melbourne. It launched Kylie Minogue, Margot Robbie, Guy Pearce and Liam Hemsworth. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neighbours>
- **Home and Away**: (Soaps · 1988) Soap set in the fictional beach town of Summer Bay (filmed at Palm Beach, Sydney). Launched Chris Hemsworth and Isla Fisher. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_and_Away>
- **MasterChef Australia**: (Reality · 2009) The most loved version of the format anywhere. The 2010 finale is one of the most watched broadcasts in Australian TV history. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MasterChef_Australia>
- **Married at First Sight**: (Reality · 2015) Strangers who marry the first time they meet. Controversial and a ratings juggernaut (the famous “MAFS”). <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Married_at_First_Sight>
- **The Block**: (Reality · 2003) Couples renovate houses that go to auction. Perfect for the national obsession with property. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Block_(Australian_TV_series)>
- **Bondi Rescue**: (Reality · 2006) A day in the life of the lifeguards at Bondi Beach, Sydney. Shown in dozens of countries. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bondi_Rescue>
- **Border Security**: (Reality · 2004) Biosecurity at the airport: that forgotten mango in your bag that turns into a fine. Explains why you declare everything on arrival. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border_Security:_Australia%27s_Front_Line>
- **Gogglebox Australia**: (Reality · 2015) Real families reacting to TV on the couch. A funny portrait of how Australians talk and think. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gogglebox_Australia>
- **Skippy**: (Nostalgia · 1968) The clever kangaroo who saved the day. A kids’ classic shown in more than 100 countries. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skippy_the_Bush_Kangaroo>
- **Hi-5**: (Nostalgia · 1999) Kids’ music and dance group that defined a 2000s childhood. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hi-5_(Australian_TV_series)>
- **Play School**: (Nostalgia · 1966) ABC kids’ show on air since 1966, one of the longest-running in the world. Big Ted and Jemima are institutions. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Play_School_(Australian_TV_series)>
- **Countdown**: (Nostalgia · 1974) ABC music show hosted by Molly Meldrum in his cowboy hat. It launched AC/DC, Kylie and many more. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countdown_(Australian_TV_program)>
- **Hey Hey It’s Saturday**: (Nostalgia · 1971) Saturday morning (later night-time) variety show with the puppet Ossie Ostrich. Ran for 28 years. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey_Hey_It%27s_Saturday>
- **Big Brother Australia**: (Nostalgia · 2001) A 2000s phenomenon, filmed at Dreamworld on the Gold Coast. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Brother_(Australian_TV_series)>
- **Australian Idol**: (Nostalgia · 2003) Launched Guy Sebastian and Jessica Mauboy. The 2003 final stopped the nation. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Idol>
- **The Simpsons**: (Nostalgia · 1991) Not Australian, but endlessly repeated on free-to-air TV. The episode “Bart vs. Australia” (1995) is legendary for sending up the country. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Simpsons>
- **The Crocodile Hunter**: (Nostalgia · 1996) The country’s most famous wildlife series, watched all over the world. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Crocodile_Hunter>
- **State of Origin**: (Big broadcasts · 1980) The yearly rugby league series between NSW (the Blues) and Queensland (the Maroons). It splits the country in two and is always among the most watched programs of the year. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_Origin_series>
- **AFL Grand Final**: (Big broadcasts) The footy decider on the last Saturday of September, with 100,000 people at the MCG. In Victoria the Friday before is a public holiday. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFL_Grand_Final>
- **Carols by Candlelight**: (Big broadcasts · 1938) The Christmas Eve candlelit concert in Melbourne, broadcast nationally since the days of radio. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carols_by_Candlelight>
- **New Year’s Eve on the Harbour**: (Big broadcasts) Sydney’s midnight fireworks over the Harbour Bridge and the Opera House, broadcast around the world. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_New_Year%27s_Eve>

Sources: [Screen Australia](https://www.screenaustralia.gov.au)

## Companies and brands

https://australianculture.biblioverse.org/brands.html

- **Qantas**: (Transport · 1920) Born in Queensland as Queensland and Northern Territory Aerial Services. One of the oldest airlines still flying, with the kangaroo on its tail. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qantas>
- **Canva**: (Tech · 2013) Founded by Perth’s Melanie Perkins and based in Sydney. A design tool used in just about every country. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canva>
- **Atlassian**: (Tech · 2002) Sydney company behind Jira, Confluence and Trello. Started on a A$10,000 credit card. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlassian>
- **Afterpay**: (Tech · 2014) Took “buy now, pay later” global. Sold in 2022 to Block (the Square company) for about US$29 billion. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afterpay>
- **BHP**: (Mining and energy · 1885) Started at the Broken Hill silver mine (NSW) and became the biggest mining company in the world. “The Big Australian”. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BHP>
- **Rio Tinto**: (Mining and energy · 1873) Anglo-Australian iron ore giant, with its big mines in the Pilbara (WA). <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_Tinto_(corporation)>
- **Commonwealth Bank**: (Banks · 1911) The country’s biggest bank, one of the “Big Four” with Westpac, NAB and ANZ. The yellow and black diamond is on every corner. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Bank>
- **Woolworths**: (Retail · 1924) The biggest supermarket chain (“Woolies”), no relation to the American Woolworth. Shares the market with Coles. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolworths_(Australia)>
- **Coles**: (Retail · 1914) The other half of the supermarket duopoly. Started in Collingwood, Melbourne. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coles_Group>
- **Bunnings**: (Retail · 1886) Hardware and garden giant, famous for the weekend sausage sizzle out the front. A Sunday outing for plenty of families. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunnings>
- **Telstra**: (Telco · 1975) The biggest phone and internet provider, formerly government-owned. The one that gets reception in the outback. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telstra>
- **Billabong**: (Fashion and surf · 1973) From the Gold Coast to the world: one of the surfwear brands that defined beachwear in the 80s and 90s. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billabong_(clothing)>
- **Rip Curl**: (Fashion and surf · 1969) Born in Torquay, gateway to the Great Ocean Road, making surfboards and wetsuits. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rip_Curl>
- **Quiksilver**: (Fashion and surf · 1969) Also from Torquay, it started with boardshorts. The logo is inspired by Hokusai’s wave. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quiksilver>
- **UGG**: (Fashion and surf · 1970s) The sheepskin boots surfers wore to warm up. In Australia “ugg” is a generic word; the global UGG brand is American. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ugg_boots>
- **R.M. Williams**: (Fashion and surf · 1932) Handmade leather boots from Adelaide, an icon of the bushman look and a favourite of politicians and King Charles. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._M._Williams>
- **Akubra**: (Fashion and surf · 1912) The wide-brimmed felt hat of the outback. Crocodile Dundee wore one. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akubra>
- **Blundstone**: (Fashion and surf · 1870) Tasmania’s Chelsea boots. From building sites to catwalks. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blundstone_Footwear>
- **Cotton On**: (Fashion and surf · 1991) Affordable fashion chain from Geelong, now in more than 15 countries. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotton_On_Group>
- **Zimmermann**: (Fashion and surf · 1991) Sisters Nicky and Simone Zimmermann took Sydney’s romantic style to Paris Fashion Week.
- **Aesop**: (Beauty · 1987) Minimalist skincare from Melbourne, with award-winning store design. Bought by L’Oréal in 2023. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aesop_(brand)>
- **Arnott’s**: (Food · 1865) The biscuit maker behind Tim Tams, Shapes and Iced VoVos, with the parrot on the logo. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnott%27s_Group>
- **Bundaberg**: (Food · 1960) Queensland’s ginger beer. The town also gives its name to the famous “Bundy” rum. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bundaberg_Brewed_Drinks>
- **Penfolds**: (Food · 1844) Adelaide winery. Its Grange is the country’s most iconic (and expensive) wine. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penfolds>
- **Holden**: (Transport · 1856) Started out making saddles and became the “national” car maker (owned by GM). The Commodore and the ute reigned until the brand closed in 2020. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holden>
- **Guzman y Gomez**: (Food · 2006) Sydney Mexican chain that became a craze and listed on the stock exchange in 2024. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guzman_y_Gomez>
- **Boost Juice**: (Food · 2000) Adelaide smoothie chain, now in more than 10 countries. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boost_Juice>
- **Westfield**: (Retail · 1959) Westfield shopping centres started in Sydney (Blacktown) and spread to the US and Europe. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westfield_Corporation>
- **Cochlear**: (Tech · 1981) World leader in hearing implants, born from Graeme Clark’s invention. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochlear_Limited>
- **CSL**: (Tech · 1916) Started as a government lab and grew into one of the biggest biotech companies in the world. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CSL_Limited>

## Food

https://australianculture.biblioverse.org/food.html


### On the plate every day

- **Fruit and veg**: Mangoes, avocados, bananas and macadamias, many of them grown right here.
- **Bread and toast**: Toast for brekkie, with Vegemite or butter.
- **Asian food**: Thai, Chinese, Vietnamese and Indian are the everyday takeaway.
- **Café coffee**: Flat whites and long blacks, never filter coffee.
- **Fish and chips**: Battered fish and chips, ideally eaten at the beach.
- **Italian and Greek**: A legacy of post-war migration, especially in Melbourne.

### Icons, dishes, sweets and drinks

- **Vegemite**: (Icons · 1923) Dark, salty yeast-extract spread created by Cyril Callister in Melbourne. Goes on buttered toast in a thin layer (very thin!). Packed with B vitamins. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vegemite>
- **Tim Tam**: (Icons · 1964) Arnott’s chocolate biscuit. The ritual is the “Tim Tam Slam”: bite off the ends and use it as a straw for coffee or hot chocolate. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Tam>
- **Anzac biscuits**: (Icons · 1915) Oat, coconut and golden syrup biscuits linked to the soldiers of World War I. The name “Anzac” is protected by law, and they must never be called “cookies”. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anzac_biscuit>
- **Pie**: (Icons · 1800s) The single-serve savoury pie with tomato sauce, the official snack of the footy. These days nearly every bakery does vegetarian and vegan versions. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meat_pie_(Australia_and_New_Zealand)>
- **Pavlova**: (Icons · 1920s) Meringue that’s crisp outside and soft inside, topped with cream and fruit. Named after the ballerina Anna Pavlova. New Zealand claims it too. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pavlova>
- **Lamington**: (Icons · 1900) A square of sponge cake dipped in chocolate and rolled in coconut. There’s even a National Lamington Day (21 July). <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamington>
- **Fairy bread**: (Icons · 1920s) White bread with butter and hundreds and thousands, cut into triangles. Compulsory at every kids’ party. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairy_bread>
- **Sausage sizzle**: (Dishes and traditions) A snag in a slice of bread (these days almost always with a veggie option), sold to raise funds at fetes, schools and on election day: the famous “democracy sausage”. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sausage_sizzle>
- **The barbie**: (Dishes and traditions) Free public electric barbecues in practically every park. Getting together around the barbie is the most Australian social occasion there is. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbecue>
- **Smashed avo**: (Dishes and traditions) Toast with smashed avocado, the symbol of Aussie brunch. A columnist famously blamed it for young people not being able to buy a house (2016). <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avocado_toast>
- **Bowen mango**: (Dishes and traditions · summer) The Queensland mango is the fruit of an Aussie Christmas: the trays hit the shops in December and everyone buys them. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kensington_Pride>
- **Damper**: (Dishes and traditions) Simple bread of flour and water baked in the coals, the food of outback travellers. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damper_(food)>
- **Christmas in summer**: (Dishes and traditions) Because Christmas falls in summer, lunch is light and cold, with salads, fruit, pavlova and ice cream, ideally at the beach or in the park. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas_in_Australia>
- **Golden Gaytime**: (Sweets and snacks · 1959) Toffee and vanilla ice cream coated in biscuit crumbs. The classic slogan: “It’s hard to have a Gaytime on your own”. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Gaytime>
- **Caramello Koala**: (Sweets and snacks) Cadbury’s koala-shaped chocolate with a caramel centre. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caramello_Koala>
- **Freddo Frog**: (Sweets and snacks · 1930) The chocolate frog of every Aussie childhood. Its price (once 20 cents) is a running joke about inflation. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddo>
- **Iced VoVo**: (Sweets and snacks) A biscuit topped with pink fondant, raspberry jam and coconut. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iced_VoVo>
- **Shapes**: (Sweets and snacks · 1976) Arnott’s savoury biscuits in flavours like Pizza and Barbecue. The 2015 recipe change caused a national uproar. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnott%27s_Shapes>
- **Twisties**: (Sweets and snacks) Cheesy corn snack, a cousin of Cheetos. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twisties>
- **Cherry Ripe**: (Sweets and snacks · 1924) The country’s oldest chocolate bar: cherry and coconut covered in dark chocolate. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherry_Ripe_(chocolate_bar)>
- **Weet-Bix**: (Sweets and snacks) Whole-wheat breakfast biscuits. “Aussie kids are Weet-Bix kids.” <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weet-Bix>
- **Milo**: (Drinks · 1934) Chocolate malt powder created in Sydney by Thomas Mayne. The best bit is the crunchy powder floating on cold milk. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milo_(drink)>
- **Flat white**: (Drinks · 1980s) Espresso with steamed milk and a thin layer of foam. Australia and New Zealand both claim it. Melbourne is the coffee capital. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flat_white>
- **Lemon, lime & bitters**: (Drinks) Lemonade with lime cordial and a few dashes of Angostura. The pub drink for when you’re not drinking. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lemon,_lime_and_bitters>
- **Bundy & Coke**: (Drinks) Bundaberg rum and Coke, with the polar bear on the bottle. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bundaberg_Rum>
- **Macadamia**: (Bush tucker (native)) Native to Queensland and NSW, it’s the only Australian native nut grown commercially around the world. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macadamia>
- **Wattleseed**: (Bush tucker (native)) Roasted acacia seed with a coffee and chocolate flavour, used by Aboriginal people for thousands of years. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wattleseed>
- **Finger lime**: (Bush tucker (native)) The “citrus caviar”: a finger-shaped lime full of tangy little pearls. A chef’s favourite. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citrus_australasica>

Sources: [Tourism Australia: food and drink](https://www.australia.com/en/things-to-do/food-and-drink.html)

## Inventions

https://australianculture.biblioverse.org/inventions.html

- **Boomerang**: (First Peoples · millennia) An aerodynamic hunting and fighting tool of Aboriginal peoples; some kinds come back to the thrower. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boomerang>
- **Woomera**: (First Peoples · millennia) A spear-thrower that adds range and power to the throw. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woomera_(spear-thrower)>
- **Didgeridoo**: (First Peoples · millennia) A wind instrument made from a trunk hollowed out by termites, from northern Australia. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Didgeridoo>
- **Mechanical refrigeration**: (Everyday life · 1856) James Harrison built one of the first ice-making machines in Geelong, paving the way for frozen exports. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Harrison_(engineer)>
- **Secret ballot**: (Society · 1856) Created in Victoria and South Australia, the “Australian ballot” was copied all over the world. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secret_ballot>
- **Aussie rules football**: (Society · 1858) Tom Wills helped write the rules to keep cricketers fit over winter. Today it’s the AFL. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_rules_football>
- **Electric drill**: (Everyday life · 1889) Arthur James Arnot and William Blanch Brain built the first one in Melbourne, to bore through rock and coal. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_James_Arnot>
- **First feature film**: (Society · 1906) The Story of the Kelly Gang, about the outlaw Ned Kelly, is considered the world’s first feature-length narrative film. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_of_the_Kelly_Gang>
- **Pacemaker**: (Health · 1926) Mark Lidwill and physicist Edgar Booth used a portable device to revive a baby in Sydney. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacemaker>
- **Penicillin at scale**: (Health · 1940s) Australian Howard Florey turned Fleming’s discovery into a medicine. A Nobel Prize in 1945 and millions of lives saved. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Florey>
- **Hills Hoist**: (Everyday life · 1945) The rotary clothesline found in every Aussie backyard. Lance Hill made it in Adelaide. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hills_Hoist>
- **Black box**: (Technology · 1956) Melbourne’s David Warren invented the cockpit voice and flight data recorder, now required in every plane. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_recorder>
- **Plastic spectacle lenses**: (Health · 1960) Developed in Adelaide by SOLA, around 60% lighter than glass. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_inventions>
- **Medical ultrasound**: (Health · 1960s) The government’s Ultrasonics Institute built pioneering imaging machines for pregnancy scans. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_ultrasound>
- **Inflatable escape slide**: (Technology · 1965) Qantas employee Jack Grant invented the inflatable evacuation slide that doubles as a raft. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evacuation_slide>
- **Cask wine**: (Everyday life · 1965) The “goon bag”: wine in a plastic bladder inside a box, invented by Tom Angove. A backpacker classic. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_wine>
- **Permaculture**: (Society · 1978) Bill Mollison and David Holmgren, from Tasmania, created the sustainable farming system now used worldwide. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permaculture>
- **Cochlear implant**: (Health · 1978) Graeme Clark created the multi-channel “bionic ear” in Melbourne, restoring hearing to hundreds of thousands of people. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochlear_implant>
- **Dual-flush toilet**: (Everyday life · 1980) Bruce Thompson at Caroma came up with the half and full flush buttons to save water. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_flush_toilet>
- **CPAP**: (Health · 1981) Sydney’s Colin Sullivan invented the mask that treats sleep apnoea. It led to the company ResMed. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_positive_airway_pressure>
- **Polymer banknotes**: (Technology · 1988) The Reserve Bank and CSIRO created the first plastic notes: longer-lasting and hard to forge. Dozens of countries now use them. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polymer_banknote>
- **Wi-Fi**: (Technology · 1992) A CSIRO team led by John O’Sullivan patented the technology that made Wi-Fi fast and reliable. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wi-Fi>
- **Spray-on skin**: (Health · 1990s) Perth’s Fiona Wood developed a spray of the patient’s own cells to treat burns. Used on victims of the 2002 Bali bombings. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiona_Wood>
- **HPV vaccine**: (Health · 2006) Ian Frazer and Chinese scientist Jian Zhou developed the technology in Brisbane for the vaccine that prevents cervical cancer. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HPV_vaccine>
- **Google Maps**: (Technology · 2005) Danish brothers Lars and Jens Rasmussen created it in Sydney at the startup Where 2, bought by Google in 2004. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Maps>

Sources: [Australia Para Todos: greatest Australian inventions](https://australiaparatodos.wordpress.com/2026/03/12/maiores-invencoes-australianas); [CSIRO](https://www.csiro.au)

## Virals and memes

https://australianculture.biblioverse.org/virals-and-memes.html


### Memes and legends

- **Drop bears**: (Legends) The “carnivorous koala” that drops out of trees onto tourists. It doesn’t exist, but every Aussie swears it does. Tip: dab Vegemite behind your ears. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drop_bear>
- **The Great Emu War**: (Legends · 1932) The Australian Army took machine guns to 20,000 emus wrecking crops in WA. The emus won. It really happened. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emu_War>
- **“Everything in Australia wants to kill you”**: (Legends) The eternal meme about spiders, snakes, jellyfish and crocs. In reality, far more people drown or die on the roads. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fauna_of_Australia>
- **Shoey**: (Behaviour) Drinking beer (or champagne) out of your own shoe. Daniel Ricciardo took the ritual to the Formula 1 podium. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drinking_from_shoes>
- **Democracy sausage**: (Behaviour) The sausage in bread sold at polling places. It was named word of the year in 2016, and there’s even a site that maps where to get one. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy_sausage>
- **Onion on top or underneath?**: (Behaviour · 2018) Bunnings told its sizzles to put the onion under the sausage “for safety” (it was slipping off). It became a national debate. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy_sausage>
- **Bin chicken**: (Behaviour) The nickname for the Australian white ibis, which raids bins in Sydney and Brisbane. Now an unofficial mascot. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_white_ibis>
- **“Throw another shrimp on the barbie”**: (Catchphrases · 1984) Paul Hogan in a tourism ad for the US. The irony: no Aussie says “shrimp”. It’s a “prawn”. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shrimp_on_the_barbie>
- **“That’s not a knife”**: (Catchphrases · 1986) “That’s not a knife. THAT’s a knife.” The Crocodile Dundee scene still gets quoted today. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crocodile_Dundee>
- **“Tell him he’s dreamin’”**: (Catchphrases · 1997) From The Castle. The standard reply to any ridiculous offer (like a price that’s way too high). <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Castle_(1997_Australian_film)>
- **“Crikey!”**: (Catchphrases) Steve Irwin’s catchcry, shorthand for Aussie enthusiasm all over the world. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Irwin>
- **“Yeah, nah”**: (Catchphrases) Means “no”. “Nah, yeah” means “yes”. And “yeah, nah, yeah”... good luck. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_English_vocabulary>
- **Bob Katter and the crocs**: (Internet · 2017) Asked about marriage equality, the MP said “let there be a thousand blossoms bloom” and then that “every three months, a person is torn to pieces by a crocodile in north Queensland”. The swerve became a meme, and a mug. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Katter>
- **“Don’t you dare say that!”**: (Internet · 2025) Bob Katter again: in August 2025, at a press conference backing anti-immigration rallies, a reporter raised his Lebanese heritage and the MP waved his fist in his face: “Don’t say that, because that irritates me, and I punch blokes in the mouth for saying that.” The clip went viral. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Katter>
- **Peggy and Molly**: (Internet · 2020) The friendship between Peggy, a staffy, and Molly, a magpie chick rescued on the Gold Coast during lockdown, won over hundreds of thousands of followers. In 2024 Molly was taken by wildlife authorities over a missing permit, and came home after a campaign by fans.
- **“Democracy manifest”**: (Internet · 1991) Jack Karlson being arrested in Brisbane after a “succulent Chinese meal”, shouting “Gentlemen, this is democracy manifest!”. The clip went viral in 2009 and became legend. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy_Manifest>
- **“Just waiting for a mate”**: (Internet) On Highway Patrol, a bloke pulled over by police answers every question with “I’m just waiting for a mate”. A classic of the Aussie internet. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_waiting_for_a_mate>
- **Corey Worthington**: (Internet · 2008) The Melbourne teenager who advertised a party on MySpace, drew 500 people and then went on TV refusing to take off his yellow sunglasses. He wouldn’t apologise, and the country never forgot.
- **“Doing a Bradbury”**: (Catchphrases · 2002) Steven Bradbury was dead last in the Winter Olympics speed skating final when everyone in front of him crashed, and he took gold. “Doing a Bradbury” means winning when nobody expected it. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Bradbury>
- **Raygun**: (Internet · 2024) University lecturer Rachael Gunn competed in breaking at the Paris Olympics with a “kangaroo hop”, scored zero and became one of the memes of the year. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachael_Gunn>
- **Dumb Ways to Die**: (Internet · 2012) Metro Trains Melbourne safety campaign with little characters dying in silly ways. It went viral and won big at Cannes. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dumb_Ways_to_Die>
- **Johnny Depp’s dogs**: (Internet · 2015) Minister Barnaby Joyce threatened to put down the actor’s dogs, brought in without quarantine. Depp and Amber Heard’s apology video became a meme. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Depp>
- **Tony Abbott’s onion**: (Internet · 2015) The then prime minister bit into a whole raw onion, skin and all, on a farm visit. Never forgotten. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Abbott>
- **Big Things**: (Internet) More than 150 giant roadside sculptures: the Big Banana, the Big Pineapple, the Big Prawn, the Big Merino... A selfie is compulsory. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_things_(Australia)>
- **Bluey**: (Internet) Scenes from the cartoon became parenting memes everywhere, and the episode “Keepy Uppy” gets used to explain adult life. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bluey_(TV_series)>

### Comedians

- **Barry Humphries**: (TV and stage) The creator of Dame Edna Everage, the cat-eye-glasses housewife who conquered London and Broadway. He died in 2023, aged 89. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_Humphries>
- **Hamish & Andy**: (TV and radio) Hamish Blake and Andy Lee, the country’s best-loved radio and TV duo, with shows, trips and podcasts. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamish_%26_Andy>
- **Kitty Flanagan**: (TV and radio) One of the country’s most popular comedians, from The Project, Utopia and her own series, Fisk. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kitty_Flanagan>
- **Wil Anderson**: (TV and radio) Stand-up and host of Gruen, the ABC show that pulls advertising apart. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wil_Anderson>
- **Tom Gleeson**: (TV and radio) The grumpy host of Hard Quiz. Won the 2019 Gold Logie with a tongue-in-cheek campaign. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Gleeson>
- **Adam Hills**: (TV and radio) Sydney-born, he also made his name in the UK as host of The Last Leg. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Hills>
- **Rove McManus**: (TV and radio) Host of the talk show Rove, a 2000s TV phenomenon. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rove_McManus>
- **Chris Lilley**: (TV and radio) Creator of Summer Heights High, We Can Be Heroes and Angry Boys, playing almost every character himself. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Lilley_(comedian)>
- **Luke McGregor**: (TV and radio) Tasmanian master of awkward, shy humour and co-creator of Rosehaven. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luke_McGregor>
- **Merrick Watts**: (TV and radio) One half of the radio duo Merrick and Rosso, a 2000s hit. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrick_Watts>
- **Hannah Gadsby**: (Stand-up) From Tasmania, a worldwide phenomenon with the Netflix special Nanette (2018). <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannah_Gadsby>
- **Carl Barron**: (Stand-up) One of the country’s most popular stand-ups, with observational comedy about everyday Aussie life. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Barron>
- **Joel Creasey**: (Stand-up) Stand-up and presenter, and SBS’s Eurovision commentator. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joel_Creasey>
- **Dilruk Jayasinha**: (Stand-up) Born in Sri Lanka, he swapped accounting for comedy and acted in the series Utopia. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dilruk_Jayasinha>
- **Ivan Aristeguieta**: (Stand-up) Venezuelan-born and Melbourne-based, he jokes about life as a migrant in Australia.
- **Isaac Butterfield**: (Stand-up) Queensland stand-up who took off on YouTube with unfiltered humour.
- **Matt Hey**: (Stand-up) Stand-up whose show clips go viral online.
- **Jimmy Rees**: (Online) Former host of Giggle and Hoot on ABC Kids who became a social media sensation with short sketches.
- **The Inspired Unemployed**: (Online) Matt Ford and Jack Steele from Byron Bay, with sketches about tradie and beach life.
- **Tanya Hennessy**: (Online) Comedian and radio host whose funny videos do the rounds online.
- **Meghan & Jack**: (Online) A couple making sketches about life together.
- **Punters Politics**: (Online) Konrad Benjamin explains Australian politics in pub language, with plenty of laughs.

Sources: [Australia Para Todos: Australian viral videos](https://australiaparatodos.wordpress.com/2025/02/01/videos-virais-australianos); [Australia Para Todos: Australian comedians](https://australiaparatodos.wordpress.com/2025/02/03/comediantes-australianos)

## National passions

https://australianculture.biblioverse.org/national-passions.html


### Customs

- **The pub**: (At the pub) A cold beer after work, a counter meal and footy on the TV. Most country towns have one, and often it’s the heart of the place.
- **Shouting a round**: (At the pub) You buy for the group and everyone takes a turn. Skipping your shout is one of the worst social crimes in the country.
- **Schooner, pot or middy?**: (At the pub) Beer glasses change name from state to state, so ordering a drink interstate can take some negotiating.
- **The barbie**: (At the table) Snags, prawns if you’re lucky, a salad someone brought and a free public barbecue in the park. One bloke holds the tongs and the whole conversation.
- **Coffee snobbery**: (At the table) A flat white from the local café, never filter. Australians will argue about the beans, and about whether it was invented here or in New Zealand.
- **Smashed avo**: (At the table) Brunch as an institution. In 2016, a columnist blamed it for young people being unable to buy houses, and the country has not let it go.
- **A pie at the servo**: (At the table) A meat pie with sauce at the petrol station or the footy. Not gourmet, and completely loved.
- **Pineapple on pizza**: (At the table) Ham and pineapple is a fixture at the local pizza shop, and many Australians order it with no shame. It was invented in Canada, and it divides dinner tables here as it does everywhere else.
- **Watching the footy**: (On screen) Which code depends on where you live, and which team often comes from your family. Plenty of people care about neither, and hear about it anyway.
- **Home and Away and Neighbours**: (On screen) Decades of beach and cul-de-sac drama, and the training ground for stars such as Kylie Minogue, Margot Robbie and Chris Hemsworth.
- **Reality TV**: (On screen) Married at First Sight, MasterChef and The Block fill the living room and the group chat. Everyone says they don’t watch, and everyone knows who got dumped.
- **The beach**: (Out and about) Esky, towel, zinc and swimming between the flags. Most Australians live near the coast, and the surf lifesaver is a national figure.
- **Slip, slop, slap**: (Out and about) The 1981 sunscreen campaign still works: slip on a shirt, slop on sunscreen, slap on a hat. Skin checks are a part of adult life.
- **Barefoot and in thongs**: (Out and about) Thongs (flip-flops) everywhere, and bare feet in the supermarket in beach towns. Visitors notice this quickly.
- **Swearing as affection**: (Out and about) Your best mate may get called a rude name, and your enemies get called “mate”. Tone is everything.
- **Tall poppy syndrome**: (Out and about) Boast about your success and you’ll be cut down to size. Being humble, or pretending to be, is the rule.
- **The backyard**: (At home) The Hills Hoist clothes line, a shed, a cricket game with a bin for stumps. It’s getting smaller, but the idea survives.
- **Bunnings and the tradie life**: (At home) The giant hardware store is a weekend outing, and tradies are its heroes: hi-vis, a ute full of tools, a 6 am start and smoko at 9. Everyone else comes for a DIY project that may never end, some pot plants and, of course, the sausage sizzle at the door.

### Sports

- **Australian rules football**: (Most followed) The national game invented in Melbourne in the 1850s. The AFL grand final stops Victoria, South Australia and Western Australia every September.
- **Rugby league**: (Most followed) The NRL rules New South Wales and Queensland, and State of Origin turns the two states into enemies for three nights. The imaginary divide with AFL is called the Barassi Line.
- **Cricket**: (Most followed) The summer soundtrack. The Boxing Day Test in Melbourne and the Ashes against England are a national ritual.
- **Rugby union**: (Most followed) The Wallabies have won two World Cups and have a fierce rivalry with New Zealand, the Bledisloe Cup.
- **The Matildas**: (Most followed) The women’s football team reached the 2023 home World Cup semi-final and captured the country, with one of the biggest TV audiences in Australian history.
- **Tennis**: (Most followed) The Australian Open fills every January. Rod Laver, Evonne Goolagong Cawley and Ash Barty are national treasures.
- **Betting**: (Most followed) Sport and gambling go hand in hand here: odds in the ad breaks, apps on phones and a flutter on the big match. Many Australians see it as part of the game, and it’s widely considered a social problem. First Nations view: Addiction groups and health experts link it to debt and family harm, and want tougher limits on gambling advertising during sport.
- **Olympic swimming**: (Most followed) Every four years, the whole country suddenly has opinions on freestyle turns. Ian Thorpe, Dawn Fraser and Ariarne Titmus lead the way.
- **Supercars**: (Most followed) V8s and the Bathurst 1000 on Mount Panorama, a race once decided by Holden against Ford.
- **Walking**: (Most played) According to the AusPlay survey, it’s the most popular activity among adults, ahead of the gym and bushwalking.
- **The gym**: (Most played) The second activity on AusPlay’s adult list. Often with an early start and a coffee afterwards.
- **Bushwalking**: (Most played) Hiking, with a local name. National parks start close to the big cities.
- **Running**: (Most played) parkrun on Saturday mornings and the City2Surf in Sydney are the great mass events.
- **Swimming**: (Most played) In pools, rock baths and the sea. Children have lessons early, and it’s among the most popular activities at every age.
- **Soccer**: (Most played) Not the most watched, but among the most played organised sports, especially among children.
- **Netball**: (Most played) For generations, the great girls’ team sport. The Diamonds are among the best teams in the world.
- **Surfing**: (Most played) More a way of life than a sport on many parts of the coast. Mick Fanning and Stephanie Gilmore made it to the top of the world.
- **Backyard cricket**: (Most played) One-hand-one-bounce, and over the fence is out. Often the most serious Christmas Day competition in the family.
- **Golf**: (Most played) The relaxed weekend option, with a cold one at the 19th hole.
- **Fishing and the races**: (Most played) Fishing is a weekend ritual from the jetty to the Top End. The races are more of a day out, in a suit or a fascinator, and many people only go for the Melbourne Cup. First Nations view: Animal rights activists criticise both, over horse deaths in racing and the suffering of fish, and hold protests and alternative events on Cup Day.

### Festivals and events

- **Anzac Day**: (Across the country) Dawn services on 25 April, then two-up in the pub, the one day it’s legal in most states. The most solemn date on the calendar, and also a big social one.
- **Melbourne Cup**: (Across the country) “The race that stops a nation”, on the first Tuesday of November. Fascinators, sweepstakes at work and 84,373 people at Flemington in 2025.
- **Hottest 100**: (Across the country) Triple j’s listener poll fills barbecues with music in late January. In 2025, a special edition of Australian songs drew over 2.6 million votes.
- **Sydney New Year’s Eve**: (Cities) Fireworks on the Harbour Bridge, seen around the world, with crowds who claim their spot from the morning.
- **Sydney Mardi Gras**: (Cities) The parade born from a 1978 protest and police violence became one of the world’s great LGBTQ+ events.
- **Vivid Sydney**: (Cities) For weeks in winter, light shows cover the Opera House and the city comes out in coats.
- **Adelaide Fringe**: (Cities) One of the world’s biggest arts festivals, turning the city into a stage every summer.
- **Beer Can Regatta**: (Cities · Darwin) Since 1974, boats made of empty beer cans have raced at Mindil Beach. It says a lot about Darwin.
- **Royal Easter Show**: (Cities) Prize cows, showbags and the farm coming to town. Every capital has its own version.
- **Garma Festival**: (The bush) Yolngu culture and national politics meet in north-east Arnhem Land every August. Prime ministers go.
- **Birdsville Races**: (The bush) Since 1882, a town of about 100 people in outback Queensland has received thousands for two days of horse racing in the dust.
- **Parkes Elvis Festival**: (The bush) Every January since 1993, a town in New South Wales fills up with Elvis impersonators, in the height of summer.
- **Tamworth Country Music Festival**: (The bush) The Australian Nashville: country music all over town each January, under the Big Golden Guitar.
- **Deni Ute Muster**: (The bush) Thousands of utes, music and mud at Deniliquin. A proud celebration of life in the country.
- **Bathurst 1000**: (The bush) The great motor race, every October on Mount Panorama. For many, it’s a camping holiday on a hill with a race in it.
- **Schoolies**: (Across the country) Teens who finish school invade the Gold Coast and other beach towns in November. Their parents try not to think about it.

### Cars

- **Holden 48-215**: (Classics · 1948) “Australia’s own car”, launched by Prime Minister Ben Chifley. It’s the car that started the love affair.
- **The ute**: (Classics · 1934) A farmer’s wife asked for a car to take to church and that could carry pigs to market. Ford Australia’s Lew Bandt designed the coupé utility, the ute.
- **Holden against Ford**: (Classics) For generations, you were one or the other, inherited like a footy team. The rivalry played out on Mount Panorama and in every pub.
- **Holden Monaro**: (Classics · 1968) The muscle car that turned heads, and which a whole generation still dreams of.
- **The Mad Max Interceptor**: (Classics · 1979) A modified Ford Falcon XB became one of cinema’s most famous cars.
- **Footy, meat pies, kangaroos and Holden cars**: (Classics) The 1970s ad jingle that summed up the national identity, and was adapted from an American one.
- **Commodore and Falcon**: (The end of an era) The family sedans that were on every street, and the cars of police and taxis for decades. Falcon production ended in 2016.
- **The end of local manufacturing**: (The end of an era · 2017) After Ford and Toyota, Holden shut its Elizabeth plant, and Australia stopped making cars. The brand itself disappeared a few years later, with plenty of grief.
- **Ford Ranger**: (Today) Best-selling vehicle in the country three years running: about 53,700 in 2025. Designed largely in Victoria, too.
- **Toyota HiLux**: (Today) The long-time king, second in 2025 with about 45,800. Tradies’ and farmers’ favourite, and now a suburban one.
- **LandCruiser**: (Today) The outback’s universal vehicle. In remote places, it’s the car that’s most likely to get you home.
- **The caravan**: (Passions) Grey nomads retire, hook up a van and drive around the country for years. The Big Lap is a real life plan.
- **Burnouts**: (Passions) Summernats, in Canberra, is the great festival of smoking tyres. Mostly a bloke thing, and very loud.
- **Bull bars and road trains**: (Passions) Roos on the road at dusk justify the bull bar, and in the outback you share the highway with trucks of three or four trailers.
- **The Kombi**: (Passions) The surfers’ van, with a board on the roof, on the way to a beach up the coast. Sought after and expensive these days.

### Internet and memes

- **A full-time job online**: (Habits) According to the Digital 2026 report, Australians spend about 41 hours a week online, against a world average of 33, including over 19 hours on social media.
- **Banning teens from social media**: (Habits · 2025) Australia became the first country with a national ban on social media accounts for under-16s. Parents, teens and platforms are still arguing about it.
- **Complaining about the NBN**: (Habits) The national broadband network has been a political fight and a source of everyday frustration for years. A shared national hobby.
- **Facebook community groups**: (Habits) Local groups for parking disputes, lost dogs, a suspicious van and people asking for a good plumber.
- **Everything wants to kill you**: (Memes) The world’s favourite Australian meme, and Australians are happy to play along. A huntsman on a car’s sun visor is a classic genre. See also Virals and memes.
- **Dry humour**: (Memes) Understatement in a deadpan voice, even in a crisis. If a local says “bit warm today” at 44 °C, that’s a joke.
- **The accent on TikTok**: (Memes) Foreigners try “g’day”, Aussies correct them and everybody disagrees on what “yeah, nah” actually means.
- **Shoey and bin chicken**: (Memes) Drinking from a shoe and an ibis stealing your chips: two local jokes that the rest of the world now gets.
- **“Australia isn’t real”**: (Abroad) A joke conspiracy theory that says the whole country is made up. Locals enjoy it, particularly since nobody believes the wildlife anyway.
- **Upside-down jokes**: (Abroad) Toilets flushing backwards, walking on the ceiling and Christmas on the beach. They’ve heard them all, and will still respond politely.
- **Celeste Barber’s bushfire fundraiser**: (Abroad · 2020) The comedian asked for donations on Facebook during Black Summer and raised over A$50 million, with money from around the world.
- **Bluey memes**: (Abroad) The Brisbane cartoon is now a language for parenthood around the world, spoken in clips and screenshots.
- **#CensusFail**: (Habits · 2016) The online census crashed on census night, and the national response was exactly what you’d expect. A bit of humour for every failure.
- **Misinformation**: (Habits) Chain posts and conspiracies have circulated here too, from the pandemic to the Voice referendum. First Nations view: During the 2023 referendum, the electoral commission spent considerable time correcting false claims about how voting works.

### The Aussie dog

- **The blue heeler**: (The dogs) The Australian cattle dog: speckled, tough and suspicious of everyone but you. Bred in the 1800s to work cattle over huge distances, with dingo in the family tree.
- **The kelpie**: (The dogs) A sheepdog who will run across the backs of a flock. Born on Australian stations from Scottish collies, and rarely still for long.
- **The dog in the back of the ute**: (The dogs) Ears in the wind, on the way to the farm or the pub. Australia’s national image of contentment (rules on tying them up apply).
- **Bluey**: (Famous dogs · 2018) A blue heeler family from Brisbane, and one of the most-watched children’s shows on the planet. Many adults admit to crying at it, alone.
- **Red Dog**: (Famous dogs) A real red kelpie cross who wandered the Pilbara in the 1970s, adopted by a whole town. He has a statue at Dampier and a hit 2011 film.
- **The Dog on the Tuckerbox**: (Famous dogs · 1932) A statue near Gundagai, from a bush poem about a loyal dog guarding a bullock driver’s lunch. A roadside stop with status.
