- **Kelpie Muster at Casterton**: (A national affection) The Victorian town that claims to be the birthplace of the kelpie holds a festival and auction, where working dogs can fetch huge prices.
- **Almost half the homes**: (A national affection) Surveys by Animal Medicines Australia found dogs in 48% of households in 2022, part of one of the world’s highest rates of pet ownership.

### And more

- **Talking about house prices**: (Everyday life) The real national sport. Any barbecue ends with what the place down the street sold for, and young people can’t afford it.
- **Coles or Woolies**: (Everyday life) Two supermarkets dominate the country, and everyone has opinions on them. Plus Aldi and a treasure hunt at Kmart.
- **Mateship**: (Everyday life) The idea of looking out for your mates, from the Anzac legend to the volunteer fire brigade. First Nations view: Historians point out that the classic mateship story centred on white men, leaving out women and First Nations people.
- **Camping**: (Everyday life) Christmas holidays at the same caravan park every year, sometimes for generations. Book early.
- **Food from everywhere**: (Everyday life) The suburban Thai, the Vietnamese pho, the Greek and Lebanese places. Migration changed the national plate, and most people are glad.
- **A sickie**: (At work) A day off “sick”, especially after a big match or a long weekend. Everyone denies it, and bosses know the pattern.
- **A beer in moderation, or not**: (Body) Drinking is part of many social events, and it’s rude to skip a round. Though younger Australians drink less than their parents. First Nations view: Doctors have long warned about the harm alcohol causes, especially for First Nations communities and in family violence.
- **Pokies**: (Money) Poker machines in clubs and pubs, especially in New South Wales. Australians are among the world’s biggest gamblers per person, and the machines take a big share. First Nations view: Addiction groups and many health experts want tougher rules on poker machines, an issue that has divided politics for years.

Sources: [AusPlay](https://www.ausport.gov.au/media-centre/news/australians-are-redefining-the-way-they-play); [Digital 2026: Australia](https://datareportal.com/reports/digital-2026-australia); [4x4 Australia: 2025 VFACTS](https://www.4x4australia.com.au/news/ford-reigns-supreme-in-2025-4x4-sales); [Victoria Racing Club](https://www.vrc.com.au/latest-news/mcc-attracts-286-000-attendees-with-spectacular-racing-and-growth-surging-across-all-event-metrics/); [Animal Medicines Australia, via Vet Voice](https://www.vetvoice.com.au/ec/pet-ownership/pet-ownership-statistics/)

## Aussie Dictionary

https://australianculture.biblioverse.org/aussie-dictionary.html

- **Ambo**: Ambulance
- **Ankle-biter**: Small child
- **Arro**: Arrogant
- **Arvo**: Afternoon
- **Aussie**: Australian
- **Aussie salute**: Waving a hand to swat away flies
- **Avo**: Avocado
- **Awks**: Awkward
- **Barbie / Barby**: Barbecue
- **Bathers**: Swimsuit
- **Berko**: Someone who gets angry for no apparent reason
- **Bevvies**: Drinks
- **Bikkie**: Biscuit
- **Bizzo**: Business
- **Bloke**: Man
- **Bloody oath**: Of course, complete agreement
- **Blotto**: Very drunk
- **Bludger**: Someone who is lazy
- **Bogan**: An uncouth or unsophisticated person
- **Bogan chic**: A mix of bogan style with fancy, fashionable things
- **Bottle-o**: Bottle shop, liquor store
- **Brekkie / Brekky**: Breakfast
- **Brolly**: Umbrella
- **Cabbie**: Taxi driver
- **Cactus**: An unpleasant, obnoxious person; also something broken
- **Chewie**: Chewing gum
- **Chockers**: Completely full
- **Chokkie**: Chocolate
- **Chook**: Chicken
- **Chrissie**: Christmas
- **Chuck**: Throw
- **Chuck on**: Put on
- **Chunder**: Throw up
- **Clanger**: An inappropriate comment
- **Coldie**: A nice, cold beer
- **Cossies**: Swimmers, swimming costume
- **Crack on**: Let’s get started, keep going
- **Crook**: Sick
- **Cunt**: Fool (very offensive, though mates may use it affectionately)
- **Cuppa**: A cup of tea or coffee
- **D’ya**: Do you
- **Daggy**: Uncool, unfashionable
- **Dead horse**: Tomato sauce
- **Defo**: Definitely
- **Devo**: Devastated, upset
- **Docos**: Documentaries
- **Dog’s eye**: Meat pie
- **Drongo**: Idiot
- **Dunny**: Toilet
- **Durry / Duzza**: Cigarette
- **Eshays**: Young troublemakers, often from the outer suburbs
- **Esky**: A portable cooler
- **Fair dinkum**: Genuine, real
- **Feed**: Meal
- **Footy / Footie**: Football (AFL or rugby league)
- **G’day**: Hello, good day
- **Galah**: A foolish person
- **Goldie**: $1 or $2 coin
- **Good on ya**: Good job, well done
- **Gorge**: Gorgeous
- **Grog**: Alcohol
- **Grouse**: Great, excellent
- **Hard yakka**: Hard work
- **Have a crack**: Give it a try
- **Heaps**: A lot
- **Hoon**: A reckless driver
- **Hooroo**: Goodbye
- **Hospo**: Hospitality (cafés, bars and restaurants)
- **Idiot box**: Television
- **Jocks**: Underwear
- **Joey**: Baby kangaroo
- **Juice**: Petrol
- **Kanga**: Kangaroo
- **Knackered**: Tired
- **Layabout**: A lazy person
- **Lippie**: Lipstick
- **Littlies**: Small children
- **Lobster**: $20 note
- **Lolly**: Sweet, candy
- **Macca’s**: McDonald’s
- **Mate**: Friend
- **Minny**: Minute
- **Moolah**: Money
- **Mozzie**: Mosquito
- **Mundy**: Monday
- **Mushies**: Mushrooms
- **Nana**: Banana
- **Narky**: Grumpy, moody
- **No drama**: No problem
- **No wozzas**: No worries
- **Noah**: Shark (from "Noah’s ark")
- **Nuke**: To microwave something
- **On the piss**: Out drinking a lot
- **Oz**: Australia
- **Ozzie**: Aussie
- **Pineapple**: $50 note
- **Pissed**: Very drunk
- **Polly**: Politician
- **Pommie / Pom**: Person from the UK
- **Port**: Suitcase or school bag
- **Prawn**: Someone who’s had a bit too much to drink
- **Preggers**: Pregnant
- **Pressie**: Present, gift
- **Ranga**: Redhead
- **Reckon**: To think, to believe ("I reckon...")
- **Rego**: Car registration
- **Righto**: OK, all right
- **Ripper**: Awesome
- **Roomie**: Roommate
- **Rubbish**: Garbage, trash
- **Sambo / Sammie / Sanga / Sanger**: Sandwich
- **Schoolies**: Celebration week for school leavers
- **Servo**: Service station, petrol station
- **Smoko**: A short break from work
- **Snag**: Sausage
- **Stick**: Surfboard
- **Stickybeak**: A nosy person
- **Stirrer**: Someone who deliberately causes trouble
- **Straya**: Australia
- **Stubby**: A small bottle of beer
- **Sundy**: Sunday
- **Sunnies**: Sunglasses
- **Ta**: Thank you
- **Thongs**: Flip-flops
- **Ticker**: Heart
- **Tinny**: Can of beer; also a small aluminium boat
- **Toddler**: A small child aged 1 to 3
- **Togs**: Swimwear
- **Tot**: A baby, toddler
- **Truckie**: Truck driver
- **Tucker**: Food
- **Ute**: Utility vehicle, pick-up
- **Wadyasay**: What did you say?
- **Wee**: Pee
- **Woofa**: Dog
- **x**: A kiss. Aussies pop an x at the end of messages, even to mates and workmates, as a friendly sign-off (“See you soon x”). The more x’s, the more affection: xx, xxx.
- **Ya**: You
- **Yonks**: A long time
- **Zonked**: Exhausted

Sources: [Australia Para Todos: Aussie terms and slang (in Portuguese)](https://australiaparatodos.wordpress.com/2025/01/29/dicionario-de-termos-e-girias-australianas/); [Brazilians in Australia: slang](https://brasileirosnaaustralia.biblioverse.org)

## Records and rankings

https://australianculture.biblioverse.org/records.html

- **Highway 1**: (Geography · 14,500 km) The longest national highway in the world, looping right around the country. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highway_1_(Australia)>
- **Nullarbor Links**: (Geography · 1,365 km) The longest golf course in the world: 18 holes spread along the Eyre Highway between SA and WA. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nullarbor_Links>
- **Dingo Fence**: (Geography · 5,614 km) The longest fence in the world, built to keep dingoes away from sheep in the south-east. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dingo_Fence>
- **90 Mile Straight**: (Geography · 146.6 km) The longest straight stretch of sealed road in the country, on the Eyre Highway. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eyre_Highway>
- **Straight railway**: (Geography · 478 km) The longest stretch of dead-straight railway in the world, across the Nullarbor Plain. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trans-Australian_Railway>
- **Great Barrier Reef**: (Nature · 2,300 km) The biggest reef system on the planet, visible from space. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Barrier_Reef>
- **K’gari (Fraser Island)**: (Nature · 1,840 km²) The biggest sand island in the world, with freshwater lakes and rainforest. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%27gari>
- **Great Artesian Basin**: (Nature · 1.7m km²) One of the largest underground water reserves in the world, beneath 22% of the country. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Artesian_Basin>
- **Oldest living culture**: (Society · 60,000+ years) Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have the oldest continuous culture on Earth. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aboriginal_Australians>
- **Biggest country**: (Rankings · 6th) 7.69 million km², and the only country that covers a whole continent. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_area>
- **Minimum wage**: (Rankings · A$26.44/hr) The national minimum wage since July 2026 (A$1,004.90 a week), one of the highest in the world. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_wage_in_Australia>
- **Nobel Prizes**: (Rankings · 15) Eight in Medicine, including Howard Florey (penicillin) and Peter Doherty (the immune system). Patrick White won for Literature in 1973. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Australian_Nobel_laureates>
- **Voter turnout**: (Society · ~90%) Voting has been compulsory since 1924 and you get fined if you don’t. The result is one of the highest turnouts in the world. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_system_of_Australia>
- **Women’s vote**: (Society · 1902) One of the first countries to give women the right to vote and stand in national elections. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women%27s_suffrage_in_Australia>
- **The MCG**: (Society · 100,024) The Melbourne Cricket Ground is the biggest stadium in the southern hemisphere and the biggest cricket ground in the world. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne_Cricket_Ground>
- **Gambling losses**: (Rankings · 1st) Australians lose more money gambling per person than anyone in the world, driven by the “pokies”. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gambling_in_Australia>
- **Most venomous snake**: (Nature · 1st) The inland taipan has the most potent venom of any land snake. It’s shy and lives far from everything. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inland_taipan>
- **Mount Augustus**: (Nature · 858 m) Often called the biggest monolith in the world, twice the size of Uluru. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Augustus_National_Park>

Sources: [Fair Work Ombudsman: minimum wages from 1 July 2026](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/about-us/workplace-laws/annual-wage-review/annual-wage-review-2026); [Wikipedia: List of Australian Nobel laureates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Australian_Nobel_laureates); [Geoscience Australia](https://www.ga.gov.au)

## Fun facts

https://australianculture.biblioverse.org/fun-facts.html

- **Official name and colours**: The official name is the Commonwealth of Australia. The national colours are green and gold, from the leaves and blossom of the golden wattle, proclaimed in 1984 and worn by the national sporting teams.
- **An anthem without God or guns**: Advance Australia Fair has no military or religious references. The 1879 original was more imperial: one verse praised Captain Cook and ended with “Britannia rules the wave”, and another called on Australians to rouse to arms. Those verses were dropped when it became the official anthem in 1984. In 2021, “young and free” became “one and free”, recognising First Nations peoples.
- **More roos than people**: There are more than 40 million kangaroos and about 28 million people.
- **Everyone’s on the coast**: Around 85% of people live within 50 km of the coast. The interior is practically empty.
- **A dry country**: Around 70% of the land is arid or semi-arid. It’s the driest inhabited continent on the planet.
- **Wider than the Moon**: From east to west Australia is about 4,000 km across. The Moon is 3,474 km in diameter.
- **The continent is moving**: The Australian plate moves about 7 cm north every year. In 2017 the country shifted its GPS coordinates by 1.8 m.
- **A capital by compromise**: Sydney and Melbourne both wanted to be the capital, so Canberra was built in between, on purpose.
- **Christmas in summer**: Santa in boardshorts, Christmas lunch at the beach and the Boxing Day Test (26 December).
- **Thongs are flip-flops**: If an Aussie says they forgot their thongs, they’re talking about their footwear.
- **Everything gets shortened**: Brekkie (breakfast), arvo (afternoon), servo (service station), avo (avocado), sunnies (sunglasses), Chrissie (Christmas).
- **No official language**: English is the main language, but no law makes it official. Before colonisation there were more than 250 Indigenous languages.
- **A third born overseas**: About 32% of the population was born in another country. Almost half have at least one parent born overseas.
- **Cube-shaped poo**: The wombat is the only animal known to make cube-shaped poo.
- **The platypus**: A mammal that lays eggs, has a duck’s bill and the males have a venomous spur. European scientists thought it was a hoax.
- **A coat of arms that doesn’t go backwards**: The kangaroo and emu are on the coat of arms, and tradition says it’s because they rarely move backwards, only forwards.
- **Slip, Slop, Slap**: The country has one of the highest skin cancer rates in the world. At school the rule is “No hat, no play”.
- **Driving on the left**: A British legacy. Pedestrians, look right first!
- **No tipping required**: Wages are high, so nobody expects a tip, though it’s appreciated at restaurants.
- **The cleanest air**: The Cape Grim station in Tasmania measures some of the purest air on the planet.
- **The PM who vanished**: Prime Minister Harold Holt disappeared while swimming in 1967. A swimming pool was later named after him.
- **Koalas sleep 20 hours**: A diet of gum leaves gives very little energy, so koalas sleep most of the day.
- **Over 10,000 beaches**: There are 10,685 beaches. Visiting one a day would take almost 30 years.
- **Biosecurity is serious**: Forgetting to declare a piece of fruit or some seeds on arrival can cost you thousands of dollars.
- **Shifting time zones**: There are three main time zones, but because QLD, WA and the NT don’t do daylight saving, in summer the country runs on five different times.

Sources: [ABS: population](https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/people/population); [Tourism Australia: Key facts](https://www.australia.com/en/facts-and-planning/about-australia/key-facts-about-australia.html); [Geoscience Australia](https://www.ga.gov.au); [Advance Australia Fair (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advance_Australia_Fair)

## Wildlife and plants

https://australianculture.biblioverse.org/wildlife-and-plants.html

- **Eastern grey kangaroo**: (Mammals) The kangaroo you’ll see most in the east, in parks, on golf courses and by the roadside at dusk. Lives in groups called “mobs”. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_grey_kangaroo>
- **Red kangaroo**: (Mammals) The biggest marsupial in the world: a male can stand over 1.8 m. Lives in the arid interior and bounds along at more than 50 km/h. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_kangaroo>
- **Wallaby**: (Mammals) Looks like a mini kangaroo. There are dozens of species, like the red-necked wallaby, common in Tasmania and the east. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallaby>
- **Koala**: (Mammals) Not a bear: a marsupial that eats almost nothing but gum leaves and sleeps up to 20 hours a day. Endangered across much of the east. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koala>
- **Wombat**: (Mammals) A sturdy marsupial that digs enormous burrows. The only animal known to make cube-shaped poo. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wombat>
- **Platypus**: (Mammals) An egg-laying mammal with a duck’s bill, and the males have a venomous spur. Lives in eastern rivers and is hard to spot. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platypus>
- **Echidna**: (Mammals) The other egg-laying mammal. Covered in spines, it eats ants and termites with a long tongue. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Echidna>
- **Quokka**: (Mammals) The “happiest animal in the world”, famous for selfies on Rottnest Island near Perth. Touching or feeding them is banned. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quokka>
- **Tasmanian devil**: (Mammals) The biggest living carnivorous marsupial, found only in Tasmania. It screeches loudly and inspired Looney Tunes’ Taz. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tasmanian_devil>
- **Brushtail possum**: (Mammals) Lives in the suburbs, in roofs and in parks. Noisy at night and easy to spot up in the trees. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_brushtail_possum>
- **Flying fox**: (Mammals) A giant fruit bat with a wingspan of up to 1 m. At sunset whole colonies cross the skies of Sydney and Brisbane. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pteropus>
- **Dingo**: (Mammals) A wild dog that arrived around 3,500 to 4,000 years ago with seafaring peoples. Today it’s considered part of the native fauna. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dingo>
- **Australian magpie**: (Birds) A black-and-white bird with a beautiful song. In spring some males swoop anyone who gets too close to the nest: it’s swooping season. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_magpie>
- **Australian white ibis**: (Birds) The “bin chicken” that raids bins in the city. Really a wetland bird that has adapted to urban life. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_white_ibis>
- **Sulphur-crested cockatoo**: (Birds) Loud and very clever. In Sydney it learned to open wheelie bins and taught the trick to other cockatoos. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulphur-crested_cockatoo>
- **Galah**: (Birds) A pink-and-grey cockatoo, common in flocks. “Galah” is also slang for a silly person. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galah>
- **Kookaburra**: (Birds) The bird whose call sounds like laughter. The natural alarm clock of many Aussie suburbs. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laughing_kookaburra>
- **Rainbow lorikeet**: (Birds) A small parrot in every colour, living in flocks in the flowering trees of eastern cities. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow_lorikeet>
- **Emu**: (Birds) The second-tallest bird in the world after the ostrich. Can’t fly but runs at 50 km/h. It’s on the national coat of arms. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emu>
- **Cassowary**: (Birds) A huge bird of the far north Queensland rainforest, with a helmet on its head. An important seed spreader. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_cassowary>
- **Brush turkey**: (Birds) Common in Brisbane and Sydney backyards. The male builds mounds of leaves that work as an incubator. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_brushturkey>
- **Australian pelican**: (Birds) Has the biggest bill of any bird in the world. Turns up on beaches, rivers and lakes right around the country. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_pelican>
- **Little penguin**: (Birds) The smallest penguin in the world, about 30 cm tall. On Phillip Island, near Melbourne, they parade ashore at dusk. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_penguin>
- **Blue-tongue lizard**: (Reptiles and others) A placid garden lizard that flashes its blue tongue when startled. Helps keep snails under control. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue-tongued_skink>
- **Goanna**: (Reptiles and others) A monitor lizard that can grow over 2 m. Common in national parks and picnic areas. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goanna>
- **Saltwater crocodile**: (Reptiles and others) The biggest living reptile in the world, in northern rivers and coastlines. Obey the signs: no swimming where there’s a warning. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saltwater_crocodile>
- **Huntsman spider**: (Reptiles and others) Big and scary-looking, but harmless to people. Often turns up inside cars and houses. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huntsman_spider>
- **Eucalyptus**: (Plants and flowers) More than 700 species of “gum trees”, the tree that defines the Aussie landscape. The smell of the bush is the smell of eucalyptus. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eucalyptus>
- **Golden wattle**: (Plants and flowers) The national floral emblem, which inspired the green and gold. It flowers at the end of winter; 1 September is Wattle Day. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acacia_pycnantha>
- **Banksia**: (Plants and flowers) Cone-shaped flowers that feed birds and marsupials. Many only release their seeds after a fire. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banksia>
- **Grevillea**: (Plants and flowers) Shrubs with curly, colourful, nectar-rich flowers. Found in almost every Aussie garden. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grevillea>
- **Waratah**: (Plants and flowers) The huge red flower that is the emblem of New South Wales. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telopea_speciosissima>
- **Kangaroo paw**: (Plants and flowers) A flower shaped like a kangaroo’s paw, the emblem of Western Australia. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anigozanthos>
- **Bottlebrush**: (Plants and flowers) Red flowers that look just like the brushes used to clean bottles. They draw in lorikeets and bees. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callistemon>
- **Paperbark**: (Plants and flowers) A tree whose bark peels off like paper. One species gives us tea tree oil, used in cosmetics. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melaleuca>
- **Grass tree**: (Plants and flowers) A plant with a dark trunk and a tuft of fine leaves that grows about 1 cm a year. Some are hundreds of years old. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xanthorrhoea>
- **Boab**: (Plants and flowers) The Australian baobab, with a fat bottle-shaped trunk, typical of the Kimberley. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adansonia_gregorii>
- **Moreton Bay fig**: (Plants and flowers) A giant fig with aerial roots, common in Sydney and Brisbane parks. Shade guaranteed. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ficus_macrophylla>
- **Wollemi pine**: (Plants and flowers) A tree from the age of the dinosaurs, known only from fossils until it was found alive in 1994 in a canyon near Sydney. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wollemia>
- **Spinifex**: (Plants and flowers) Spiky grass that covers much of the outback and holds the red desert sand in place. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triodia_(plant)>
- **Macadamia**: (Plants and flowers) A tree native to Queensland and NSW. The world’s most famous Australian nut. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macadamia>
- **Bilby**: (Mammals) A long-eared desert marsupial. At Easter, plenty of Aussies swap the chocolate bunny for a chocolate bilby. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_bilby>
- **Sugar glider**: (Mammals) A small nocturnal possum that glides from tree to tree on a membrane stretched between its legs. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar_glider>
- **Numbat**: (Mammals) A striped marsupial that eats thousands of termites a day. Western Australia’s emblem, and endangered. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbat>
- **Tree-kangaroo**: (Mammals) Yes, some kangaroos live in trees. Lumholtz’s tree-kangaroo lives in the rainforests of far north Queensland. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tree-kangaroo>
- **Superb fairywren**: (Birds) A tiny bird; in breeding season the male turns electric blue. Common in gardens and parks. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superb_fairywren>
- **Black swan**: (Birds) Europeans thought black swans didn’t exist until they saw Australia’s. It’s the emblem of Western Australia. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_swan>
- **Willie wagtail**: (Birds) Small, black and white and not the least bit shy. Wags its tail from side to side non-stop. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_wagtail>
- **Tawny frogmouth**: (Birds) Looks like an owl but isn’t. By day it sits dead still on a branch, disguised as a bit of tree. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tawny_frogmouth>
- **Superb lyrebird**: (Birds) The bird world’s greatest mimic: it copies other birds, chainsaws and camera shutters. It’s on the 10-cent coin. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superb_lyrebird>
- **Wedge-tailed eagle**: (Birds) Australia’s biggest bird of prey, soaring high over the outback. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wedge-tailed_eagle>
- **Crimson rosella**: (Birds) A red-and-blue parrot of the eastern forests and a regular at mountain picnics. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimson_rosella>
- **Frill-necked lizard**: (Reptiles and others) Flares a huge frill around its head to scare off anyone who gets too close. It used to be on the 2-cent coin. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frilled_lizard>
- **Green tree frog**: (Reptiles and others) A chubby, smiley frog that loves turning up in Queensland bathrooms and water tanks. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_green_tree_frog>
- **Thorny devil**: (Reptiles and others) A spiky desert lizard that drinks through its skin, along channels that carry water to its mouth. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thorny_devil>
- **Humpback whale**: (Marine life) Between May and November, tens of thousands migrate along the east and west coasts. You can spot them from the beach. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humpback_whale>
- **Green sea turtle**: (Marine life) Nests on Great Barrier Reef beaches. The hatchlings race to the sea at night. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_sea_turtle>
- **Dugong**: (Marine life) The “sea cow” that grazes on seagrass in places like Moreton Bay and Shark Bay. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dugong>
- **Leafy seadragon**: (Marine life) A seahorse relative that looks like floating seaweed. South Australia’s marine emblem. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leafy_seadragon>
- **Sturt’s desert pea**: (Plants and flowers) A red flower with a glossy black centre that paints the desert. South Australia’s floral emblem. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swainsona_formosa>
- **Cooktown orchid**: (Plants and flowers) A purple orchid from the northern forests, Queensland’s floral emblem. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dendrobium_bigibbum>
- **Common heath**: (Plants and flowers) A shrub with little bell-shaped pink or white flowers. Victoria’s floral emblem. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epacris_impressa>
- **Sturt’s desert rose**: (Plants and flowers) A mauve flower of the arid lands, the Northern Territory’s floral emblem. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gossypium_sturtianum>
- **Tasmanian blue gum**: (Plants and flowers) A tall tree with bluish leaves, Tasmania’s floral emblem and one of the most planted trees in the world. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eucalyptus_globulus>
- **Royal bluebell**: (Plants and flowers) A little blue grassland flower, the ACT’s floral emblem. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wahlenbergia_gloriosa>
- **River red gum**: (Plants and flowers) The giant eucalypt that lines inland rivers. It can live for more than 500 years. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eucalyptus_camaldulensis>
- **Tree fern**: (Plants and flowers) Ferns with trunks several metres tall, typical of the cool forests of the south-east and Tasmania. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dicksonia_antarctica>
- **Lilly pilly**: (Plants and flowers) A tree with edible pink berries, very popular as a backyard hedge. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syzygium>
- **Queensland bottle tree**: (Plants and flowers) A fat, bottle-shaped trunk where the tree stores water for the dry. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brachychiton_rupestris>

Sources: [Atlas of Living Australia](https://www.ala.org.au); [Australian Museum](https://australian.museum); [Australian National Botanic Gardens](https://www.anbg.gov.au)

## Major cities

https://australianculture.biblioverse.org/cities.html

- **Greater Sydney**: NSW: 5,450,496 people. Aboriginal name: Gadi (Gadigal)
- **Greater Melbourne**: VIC: 5,207,145 people. Aboriginal name: Naarm (Wurundjeri and Bunurong)
- **Greater Brisbane**: QLD: 2,706,966 people. Aboriginal name: Meanjin (Turrbal and Yuggera)
- **Greater Perth**: WA: 2,309,338 people. Aboriginal name: Boorloo (Whadjuk Noongar)
- **Greater Adelaide**: SA: 1,446,380 people. Aboriginal name: Tarntanya (Kaurna)
- **Gold Coast**: QLD: 666,087 people. Aboriginal name: None (Yugambeh)
- **Canberra**: ACT: 466,566 people. Aboriginal name: Kanbarra (Ngunnawal and Ngambri)
- **Sunshine Coast**: QLD: 365,942 people. Aboriginal name: None (Kabi Kabi and Jinibara)
- **Central Coast**: NSW: 351,934 people. Aboriginal name: None (Darkinjung)
- **Greater Geelong**: VIC: 282,809 people. Aboriginal name: Djilang (Wadawurrung)
- **Greater Hobart**: TAS: 253,654 people. Aboriginal name: nipaluna (muwinina)
- **Wollongong**: NSW: 219,141 people. Aboriginal name: None (Dharawal)
- **Townsville**: QLD: 201,433 people. Aboriginal name: Gurambilbarra (Wulgurukaba and Bindal)
- **Toowoomba**: QLD: 181,821 people. Aboriginal name: None (Jarowair and Giabal)
- **Cairns**: QLD: 175,398 people. Aboriginal name: Gimuy (Yidinji)
- **Newcastle**: NSW: 174,294 people. Aboriginal name: Mulubinba (Awabakal and Worimi)
- **Greater Darwin**: NT: 150,736 people. Aboriginal name: Garramilla (Larrakia)
- **Mackay**: QLD: 126,907 people. Aboriginal name: None (Yuwibara)
- **Greater Bendigo**: VIC: 124,174 people. Aboriginal name: None (Dja Dja Wurrung)
- **Ballarat**: VIC: 118,137 people. Aboriginal name: None (Wadawurrung)
- **Bundaberg**: QLD: 104,166 people. Aboriginal name: None (Taribelang Bunda and Gooreng Gooreng)
- **Port Macquarie-Hastings**: NSW: 89,596 people. Aboriginal name: None (Birpai)
- **Rockhampton**: QLD: 84,517 people. Aboriginal name: None (Darumbal)
- **Coffs Harbour**: NSW: 80,489 people. Aboriginal name: None (Gumbaynggirr)
- **Launceston**: TAS: 71,788 people. Aboriginal name: None (palawa)

### The personality of each capital

- **Sydney**: (NSW · Harbour City) The biggest and the priciest. The Opera House, the Harbour Bridge, Bondi and Manly. Founded in 1788, it’s the oldest city in the country.
- **Melbourne**: (VIC · Cultural capital) Coffee, graffitied laneways, trams and sport (AFL, the Australian Open, the F1 and cricket at the MCG). Four seasons in one day.
- **Brisbane**: (QLD · Brisvegas) Sunshine all year and a more relaxed pace. Host of the 2032 Olympics.
- **Perth**: (WA · The isolated capital) One of the most isolated big cities in the world, with empty beaches and a mining economy. Rottnest’s quokkas are just offshore.
- **Adelaide**: (SA · City of Churches) Planned, laid-back and surrounded by wine regions (the Barossa, McLaren Vale). Home to the Fringe, one of the biggest arts festivals in the world.
- **Gold Coast**: (QLD · Glitter Strip) Beachfront high-rises, theme parks and surf.
- **Canberra**: (ACT · The planned capital) Designed by American architects Walter and Marion Griffin. Parliament, national museums and plenty of nature.
- **Hobart**: (TAS · Gateway to Antarctica) The second-oldest city, at the foot of kunanyi/Mount Wellington. Home to the MONA museum and the Dark Mofo winter festival.
- **Darwin**: (NT · The Top End) Tropical, with a wet and a dry season, crocs and sunsets at the Mindil Beach markets. Closer to Asia than to Sydney.

Sources: [ABS: Regional population (2023)](https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/people/population/regional-population/latest-release); [Brazilians in Australia: Get to know Australia](https://brasileirosnaaustralia.biblioverse.org)

## Places

https://australianculture.biblioverse.org/places.html

- **Bondi Beach**: (Beaches · NSW) The country’s most famous beach, 7 km from the Sydney CBD. Home to the Icebergs ocean pool, the lifeguards of Bondi Rescue and the 6 km coastal walk to Coogee. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bondi_Beach>
- **Whitehaven Beach**: (Beaches · QLD) Seven kilometres of almost pure silica sand in the Whitsundays. From the Hill Inlet lookout, the tide swirls white sand through turquoise water. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitehaven_Beach>
- **Manly Beach**: (Beaches · NSW) Half an hour by ferry from Circular Quay, past the Opera House. A surf beach with the Corso promenade and a proper beach-town feel. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manly_Beach>
- **Bells Beach**: (Beaches · VIC) A legendary break near Torquay, at the start of the Great Ocean Road. Every Easter it hosts the Rip Curl Pro, one of the world’s most storied surf contests. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bells_Beach>
- **Byron Bay**: (Beaches · NSW) Surf town with an alternative streak. The Cape Byron lighthouse marks the most easterly point of mainland Australia. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byron_Bay>
- **Cable Beach**: (Beaches · WA) 22 km of white sand at Broome in the north-west. Sunset over the Indian Ocean is the main event of the day. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cable_Beach>
- **Cottesloe Beach**: (Beaches · WA) Perth’s beach, with calm water and sunsets over the sea. Every year it hosts the open-air Sculpture by the Sea exhibition. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cottesloe_Beach>
- **Hyams Beach**: (Beaches · NSW) On Jervis Bay, south of Sydney, it’s famous for its dazzling white sand and crystal-clear water. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyams_Beach>
- **Wineglass Bay**: (Beaches · TAS) The wineglass-shaped bay in Freycinet National Park. The track up to the lookout is one of Tasmania’s most photographed walks. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freycinet_National_Park>
- **Surfers Paradise**: (Beaches · QLD) The heart of the Gold Coast: high-rises right on the sand, waves all year and a lively nightlife. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surfers_Paradise>
- **Rottnest Island**: (Beaches · WA) Wadjemup to the Noongar people. A car-free island 18 km off Fremantle, explored by bike between bays of crystal-clear water. Home of the quokkas, famous for selfies where they seem to smile. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rottnest_Island>
- **Uluṟu-Kata Tjuṯa**: (Parks · NT) Country of the Anangu, the Traditional Owners. Uluru stands 348 m high and climbing it has been banned since 2019 out of respect; nearby, Kata Tjuta is a cluster of 36 rock domes. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulu%E1%B9%9Fu-Kata_Tju%E1%B9%AFa_National_Park>
- **Kakadu**: (Parks · NT) The country’s second-biggest national park (after Munga-Thirri–Simpson Desert), World Heritage-listed for both nature and culture. Ubirr and Burrungkuy hold Aboriginal rock art thousands of years old. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kakadu_National_Park>
- **Blue Mountains**: (Parks · NSW) Two hours from Sydney, with the Three Sisters rock formation and the blue haze rising off the gum trees. World Heritage-listed since 2000. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mountains_(New_South_Wales)>
- **Daintree Rainforest**: (Parks · QLD) One of the oldest rainforests on Earth. At Cape Tribulation, the forest runs right down to the sea and the Great Barrier Reef. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daintree_Rainforest>
- **Royal National Park**: (Parks · NSW) Created in 1879, it’s the world’s second-oldest national park after Yellowstone. On Sydney’s southern edge, with clifftop walks and rock pools. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Park>
- **Cradle Mountain**: (Parks · TAS) Jagged peaks above Dove Lake. It’s the start of the Overland Track, a 65 km hike through Tasmania’s wilderness. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cradle_Mountain-Lake_St_Clair_National_Park>
- **Gariwerd (Grampians)**: (Parks · VIC) Sandstone ranges in western Victoria, with lookouts like the Pinnacle and the Balconies and many Aboriginal rock art sites. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grampians_National_Park>
- **Karijini**: (Parks · WA) Deep red gorges in the Pilbara, with natural pools and waterfalls tucked between rock walls billions of years old. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karijini_National_Park>
- **Kings Park**: (Parks · WA) One of the biggest inner-city parks in the world, larger than New York’s Central Park, looking over the Perth CBD and the Swan River. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kings_Park,_Western_Australia>
- **Royal Botanic Garden Sydney**: (Parks · NSW) Opened in 1816 next to the Opera House. From Mrs Macquarie’s Chair you get the bridge and the Opera House in one shot. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Botanic_Garden,_Sydney>
- **South Bank and Streets Beach**: (Parks · QLD) Riverside parklands on the old Expo 88 site in Brisbane, home to Streets Beach: a man-made beach with sand and a lagoon right in the city, free and patrolled by lifeguards. Across the river sits Queen’s Wharf, the precinct with The Star casino, hotels and restaurants. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Bank_Parklands>
- **Great Barrier Reef**: (Natural wonders · QLD) The world’s largest coral reef system, around 2,300 km long. World Heritage-listed since 1981 and visible from space. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Barrier_Reef>
- **Twelve Apostles**: (Natural wonders · VIC) Limestone stacks rising out of the sea along the Great Ocean Road. Despite the name, only seven are still standing: erosion knocks them down one by one. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twelve_Apostles_(Victoria)>
- **K’gari**: (Natural wonders · QLD) The world’s largest sand island, formerly Fraser Island. In 2023 it officially went back to its Butchulla name, which means “paradise”. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%27gari>
- **The Pinnacles**: (Natural wonders · WA) Thousands of limestone pillars scattered across the yellow sand of Nambung National Park, north of Perth. It looks like another planet. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pinnacles_(Western_Australia)>
- **Lake Hillier**: (Natural wonders · WA) A bubblegum-pink lake on Middle Island in the Recherche Archipelago. The colour comes from algae and bacteria living in the salty water. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Hillier>
- **Wave Rock**: (Natural wonders · WA) A 15-metre granite wall shaped like a wave about to break, near the small town of Hyden. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wave_Rock>
- **Purnululu (Bungle Bungle)**: (Natural wonders · WA) Beehive-shaped sandstone domes striped orange and black, in the Kimberley. The wider world only learned of them in the 1980s; they’re now World Heritage-listed. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purnululu_National_Park>
- **Ikara (Wilpena Pound)**: (Natural wonders · SA) A vast natural amphitheatre of mountains in the Flinders Ranges, a sacred place for the Adnyamathanha people. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilpena_Pound>
- **Whitsunday Islands**: (Natural wonders · QLD) Seventy-four islands in the middle of the Great Barrier Reef, made for sailing, snorkelling and Whitehaven Beach. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitsunday_Islands>
- **Sydney Opera House**: (Buildings · NSW) Opened in 1973, with sails designed by Danish architect Jørn Utzon. World Heritage-listed since 2007 and the symbol of the nation. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Opera_House>
- **Parliament House**: (Buildings · ACT) Canberra’s parliament, opened in 1988, is built into a hill with a grassed roof you can walk over. On top sits an 81-metre flagpole. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_House,_Canberra>
- **Flinders Street Station**: (Buildings · VIC) The yellow 1910 station is Melbourne’s postcard. “Meet you under the clocks” is the city’s classic meeting spot. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flinders_Street_railway_station>
- **Royal Exhibition Building**: (Buildings · VIC) An 1880 exhibition palace in Melbourne, where the first federal parliament sat in 1901. World Heritage-listed since 2004. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Exhibition_Building>
- **Queen Victoria Building**: (Buildings · NSW) An 1898 shopping arcade in the Sydney CBD, with domes, stained glass and mechanical clocks. It was nearly demolished in the 1950s. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Victoria_Building>
- **Federation Square**: (Buildings · VIC) A 2002 cultural square opposite Flinders Street, with geometric facades, galleries and a big screen for major events. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_Square>
- **Sydney Tower Eye**: (Buildings · NSW) At 309 metres, the tallest structure in Sydney since 1981. From the deck you can see from the ocean to the Blue Mountains. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Tower>
- **Q1**: (Buildings · QLD) A 322-metre residential tower in Surfers Paradise, with the SkyPoint observation deck up top and views of the whole Gold Coast. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Q1_(building)>
- **MONA**: (Buildings · TAS) Hobart’s Museum of Old and New Art, opened in 2011 and dug into the rock beside the Derwent River. Deliberately provocative. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Old_and_New_Art>
- **Sydney Harbour Bridge**: (Bridges · NSW) The “Coathanger”, opened in 1932, is one of the world’s largest steel arch bridges. You can walk over the arch on the BridgeClimb, 134 m above the water, and it’s the centrepiece of the New Year’s Eve fireworks. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Harbour_Bridge>
- **Story Bridge**: (Bridges · QLD) A 1940 steel bridge over the Brisbane River and the city’s postcard. It has a guided climb too. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Story_Bridge>
- **West Gate Bridge**: (Bridges · VIC) The bridge over the Yarra in Melbourne. During construction in 1970 a span collapsed, killing 35 workers: Australia’s worst industrial accident. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Gate_Bridge>
- **Anzac Bridge**: (Bridges · NSW) A 1995 cable-stayed bridge in Sydney, with statues of an Australian and a New Zealand soldier honouring the Anzacs. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anzac_Bridge>
- **Sea Cliff Bridge**: (Bridges · NSW) A bridge that curves around the cliff out over the ocean, on the Grand Pacific Drive near Wollongong. Straight out of a car ad. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Cliff_Bridge>
- **Richmond Bridge**: (Bridges · TAS) Built by convicts in 1823, it’s the oldest stone bridge still in use in Australia. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond_Bridge_(Tasmania)>
- **Kurilpa Bridge**: (Bridges · QLD) A 2009 footbridge in Brisbane with masts and cables at wild angles. It’s the world’s largest tensegrity bridge. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurilpa_Bridge>
- **Tasman Bridge**: (Bridges · TAS) It links the two sides of Hobart. In 1975 a ship hit its pylons and brought down part of the bridge, splitting the city for nearly two years. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tasman_Bridge>
- **Australian War Memorial**: (Monuments · ACT) Canberra’s memorial and museum, opened in 1941. Every afternoon the Last Post Ceremony tells the story of one name on the Roll of Honour. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_War_Memorial>
- **Shrine of Remembrance**: (Monuments · VIC) Melbourne’s 1934 war memorial. At 11 am on 11 November, a ray of sunlight falls through the roof onto the word “Love” on the Stone of Remembrance. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shrine_of_Remembrance>
- **Great Ocean Road**: (Monuments · VIC) 243 km of coastal road built by soldiers returned from the First World War. It’s the largest war memorial in the world. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Ocean_Road>
- **Aboriginal Tent Embassy**: (Monuments · ACT) Set up in 1972 outside Old Parliament House to demand land rights. It’s one of the longest-running protest sites in the world. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aboriginal_Tent_Embassy>
- **Port Arthur**: (Monuments · TAS) A former convict settlement from 1830, now a historic site. Part of the World Heritage-listed Australian Convict Sites. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Arthur,_Tasmania>
- **Fremantle Prison**: (Monuments · WA) A prison built by convicts in the 1850s and used until 1991. Also part of the World Heritage-listed Australian Convict Sites. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fremantle_Prison>
- **Old Parliament House**: (Monuments · ACT) Home of federal parliament from 1927 to 1988, in Canberra. It now houses the Museum of Australian Democracy. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Parliament_House,_Canberra>
- **Big Banana**: (Big Things · NSW) Coffs Harbour’s giant banana, from 1964, kicked off the Big Things craze: there are now more than 150 oversized roadside sculptures around the country. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Banana>
- **Big Pineapple**: (Big Things · QLD) A 16-metre pineapple on the Sunshine Coast, opened in 1971. Prince Charles and Princess Diana even dropped by. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Pineapple>
- **Golden Guitar**: (Big Things · NSW) A 12-metre golden guitar in Tamworth, the home of Australian country music, where the Tamworth Country Music Festival runs every January. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Golden_Guitar>

Sources: [Tourism Australia: places to go](https://www.australia.com/en/places.html); [Parks Australia](https://parksaustralia.gov.au); [UNESCO: World Heritage in Australia](https://whc.unesco.org/en/statesparties/au); [Australia’s big things (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia%27s_big_things)

## Moments in history

https://australianculture.biblioverse.org/history.html

- **The First Peoples**: (First Peoples · 65,000–50,000 BC) The ancestors of Aboriginal people arrive on the continent. The oldest continuous living culture on Earth begins, with hundreds of nations and languages.
- **The Dutch**: (Colonisation · 1606) Willem Janszoon, aboard the Duyfken, is the first recorded European to set foot in Australia, on Cape York.
- **James Cook**: (Colonisation · 1770) The British captain charts the east coast, lands at Botany Bay and claims the land for the Crown.
- **The First Fleet**: (Colonisation · 26 Jan 1788) Eleven ships carrying about 1,400 people, half of them convicts, found the penal colony at Sydney Cove. The date is Australia Day, which many Indigenous people call Invasion Day.
- **A convict colony**: (Colonisation · 1788–1868) Around 162,000 convicts are transported from Britain. The last ship arrives in Western Australia in 1868.
- **The gold rush**: (Nation · 1851) Gold in NSW and Victoria sends the population soaring and makes Melbourne one of the richest cities in the world.
- **Eureka Stockade**: (Nation · 1854) Miners at Ballarat rebel against the colonial government. The uprising is seen as the birthplace of Australian democracy.
- **Ned Kelly**: (Nation · 1880) The outlaw in iron armour is hanged in Melbourne and becomes a national legend.
- **Federation**: (Nation · 1 Jan 1901) The six colonies unite to form the Commonwealth of Australia. The same year, the White Australia policy begins.
- **Votes for women**: (Nation · 1902) Women (but not Indigenous women) win the right to vote and stand in federal elections.
- **Gallipoli**: (War · 25 Apr 1915) ANZAC troops land in Turkey. The defeat becomes a founding myth; 25 April is Anzac Day.
- **Harbour Bridge**: (Nation · 1932) Sydney’s bridge opens. The same year, the Great Emu War takes place.
- **Darwin bombed**: (War · 1942) In World War II Japan attacks Darwin, the biggest foreign attack ever on Australian soil.
- **“Populate or perish”**: (Society · 1945) Mass post-war migration begins, with British, Italian, Greek and other European arrivals. More than 7 million people would come in the following decades.
- **Melbourne Olympics**: (Society · 1956) The first Games in the southern hemisphere. Television arrives the same year.
- **The dollar arrives**: (Society · 1966) Decimal currency replaces the Australian pound.
- **A historic referendum**: (First Peoples · 1967) 90.77% vote for Aboriginal people to be counted in the Census and covered by federal laws.
- **White Australia ends**: (Society · 1973) The Whitlam government finally abandons race-based immigration policy. The Opera House opens.
- **The Dismissal**: (Nation · 1975) The Governor-General sacks Prime Minister Gough Whitlam, the country’s biggest constitutional crisis.
- **America’s Cup**: (Society · 1983) Australia II ends 132 years of American dominance in the race. PM Bob Hawke says any boss who sacks someone for not turning up to work that day “is a bum”.
- **Australia Act**: (Nation · 1986) The last legal ties with the British Parliament are cut.
- **The Mabo decision**: (First Peoples · 1992) The High Court overturns the idea of “terra nullius” (nobody’s land) and recognises native title.
- **Port Arthur and guns**: (Society · 1996) After 35 people are killed in Tasmania, the country passes strict gun laws, with a buyback of 650,000 firearms.
- **The republic referendum**: (Nation · 1999) Voters reject swapping the monarchy for a republic. The British monarch remains head of state.
- **Sydney Olympics**: (Society · 2000) Aboriginal athlete Cathy Freeman lights the cauldron and wins the 400 m.
- **The Apology**: (First Peoples · 2008) PM Kevin Rudd apologises to the Stolen Generations, Indigenous children taken from their families.
- **Marriage equality**: (Society · 2017) After a postal survey returns 61.6% “yes”, same-sex marriage becomes law.
- **Black Summer**: (Society · 2019–20) Bushfires burn more than 24 million hectares and kill or displace around 3 billion animals.
- **The Matildas and the Voice**: (First Peoples · 2023) The women’s team reaches the World Cup semi-final at home and stops the nation. In October, the referendum on an Indigenous Voice to Parliament is defeated.
- **Olympic Brisbane**: (Society · 2032) Brisbane will be the third Australian city to host the Olympic Games.

Sources: [National Museum of Australia: Defining Moments](https://www.nma.gov.au/defining-moments); [AIATSIS](https://aiatsis.gov.au)

## Key dates

https://australianculture.biblioverse.org/key-dates.html

- **New Year and Federation**: (Public holidays · 1 January) The year opens with fireworks over the Harbour Bridge and the Opera House, watched around the world. It also marks Federation: on 1 January 1901 the six colonies united and the Commonwealth of Australia was born. First Nations view: The 1901 Constitution said Aboriginal people were not to be counted in the population. That clause only went in the 1967 referendum. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Australia>
- **Australia Day**: (Public holidays · 26 January) National public holiday marking the arrival of the First Fleet at Sydney Cove in 1788. Expect barbies, the beach, citizenship ceremonies and, the evening before, the Australian of the Year announcement. First Nations view: For many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people it is Invasion Day or Survival Day, with marches around the country. The protest goes back a long way: 26 January 1938 was the Day of Mourning in Sydney. The push to change the date keeps growing, and in 2018 triple j moved its Hottest 100 off the day. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia_Day>
- **Anniversary of the Apology**: (First Nations dates · 13 February) On 13 February 2008 Prime Minister Kevin Rudd apologised in Parliament to the Stolen Generations: Aboriginal children taken from their families under government policy. The day is marked every year. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apology_to_Australia%27s_Indigenous_peoples>
- **Sydney Mardi Gras**: (Culture and community · February or March) The LGBTQIA+ parade down Oxford Street, one of the biggest in the world. It began in 1978 as a protest, when dozens of marchers were arrested by police. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Gay_and_Lesbian_Mardi_Gras>
- **Clean Up Australia Day**: (Culture and community · First Sunday in March) Volunteers across the country pick up rubbish from beaches, parks and rivers. It started in 1989 with sailor Ian Kiernan, appalled by the rubbish he saw at sea. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clean_Up_Australia>
- **Labour Day**: (Public holidays · March, May or October) The workers’ holiday falls on different dates in each state. It celebrates the eight-hour day, won by Melbourne stonemasons in 1856, one of the first in the world. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Day>
- **Harmony Day**: (Culture and community · 21 March) A day celebrating cultural diversity, with schools and offices dressed in orange. It falls on the UN International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination. First Nations view: Critics, including First Nations leaders, say the name “harmony” softens the day and takes the focus off fighting racism, which was the UN’s point. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony_Day>
- **Easter**: (Public holidays · March or April) A long weekend from Good Friday to Easter Monday. Alongside the bunny there’s the chocolate bilby: rabbits are a pest here, and the bilby is a threatened native marsupial. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easter>
- **Anzac Day**: (Remembrance · 25 April) The country’s most solemn day remembers the Gallipoli landing in 1915 and everyone who has served. It starts with dawn services and carries on with marches and two-up in the pubs. First Nations view: Aboriginal soldiers fought in the world wars and came home to be shut out of the land and benefits other veterans got. Many also want the Frontier Wars, fought between settlers and Aboriginal peoples, remembered like other wars. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anzac_Day>
- **Mother’s Day**: (Culture and community · Second Sunday in May) Breakfast in bed and flowers. The traditional flower is the chrysanthemum: it blooms in May, and its nickname, mum, says it all. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mother%27s_Day>
- **National Sorry Day**: (First Nations dates · 26 May) A day to remember the Stolen Generations, held since 1998, a year after the Bringing Them Home report revealed the scale of the removals. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Sorry_Day>
- **National Reconciliation Week**: (First Nations dates · 27 May to 3 June) A week for building relationships between all Australians and First Nations peoples. The dates mark two wins: the 1967 referendum (27 May) and the 1992 Mabo decision (3 June), which recognised native title. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Reconciliation_Week>
- **King’s Birthday**: (Public holidays · Second Monday in June) A holiday for the monarch, in June in most states (Queensland and WA use other dates). It isn’t King Charles III’s actual birthday, which is in November. First Nations view: For many First Nations people the Crown is where colonisation began, and the day tends to bring up the debate about Australia becoming a republic. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King%27s_Official_Birthday>
- **NAIDOC Week**: (First Nations dates · First week of July) The big celebration of the history, culture and achievements of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, with events all over the country. Its roots go back to the protests of 1938. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAIDOC_Week>
- **Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children’s Day**: (First Nations dates · 4 August) Celebrating First Nations children since 1988. The date was chosen because many Stolen Generations children never knew their birthday and celebrated on this day.
- **Father’s Day**: (Culture and community · First Sunday in September) Celebrated in spring, on the first Sunday in September, with breakfasts, barbies and the footy. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Father%27s_Day>
- **R U OK? Day**: (Culture and community · Second Thursday in September) A day to ask family, friends and workmates: “Are you OK?” Started in 2009 to help prevent suicide and get people talking about mental health. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R_U_OK%3F>
- **AFL Grand Final**: (Culture and community · Late September) The Aussie rules decider at the MCG in Melbourne. In Victoria, the Friday before the game is a public holiday. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFL_Grand_Final>
- **Remembrance Day**: (Remembrance · 11 November) At 11 am the country stops for a minute’s silence, the hour the First World War ended in 1918. People wear red poppies on their lapels. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remembrance_Day>
- **Christmas**: (Public holidays · 25 December) Christmas in summer: the beach, the pool, pavlova and Carols by Candlelight in Melbourne. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas_in_Australia>
- **Boxing Day**: (Public holidays · 26 December) Sales day, the Boxing Day Test at the MCG and the start of the Sydney to Hobart yacht race, with the harbour full of boats. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boxing_Day_Test>

Sources: [Australian Government: public holidays](https://www.australia.gov.au/public-holidays); [Reconciliation Australia](https://www.reconciliation.org.au); [NAIDOC](https://www.naidoc.org.au); [AIATSIS](https://aiatsis.gov.au)

## Politics and economy

https://australianculture.biblioverse.org/politics-and-economy.html


### How it works

- **A monarchy that runs like a republic**: (Structure) The head of state is King Charles III, represented here by the Governor-General (Sam Mostyn, since 2024). The role is ceremonial: the Prime Minister actually runs the country. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Australia>
- **Three levels of government**: (Structure) The federal government in Canberra handles defence, immigration, Medicare and income tax. The states and territories run schools, hospitals, police and transport. Local councils look after bins, parks and libraries. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federalism_in_Australia>
- **Two houses of Parliament**: (Structure) The House of Representatives has 150 members and decides who governs. The Senate has 76 senators, 12 per state and 2 per territory, and reviews the laws. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Australia>
- **The Prime Minister**: (Structure) Leads the party with a majority in the House. Since May 2022 that’s Anthony Albanese of the Labor Party, re-elected comfortably in 2025. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Australia>
- **The Westminster model**: (Structure) Inherited from the UK: ministers sit in Parliament and face questions from the Opposition every sitting day, in Question Time. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_system>
- **Compulsory voting**: (Elections) Since 1924 every adult citizen has to vote or cop a fine. Elections are always on a Saturday, democracy sausage included. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_system_of_Australia>
- **Preferential voting**: (Elections) Voters number the candidates in order of preference. If nobody gets more than half, the lowest drop out and their votes flow to the next choice. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instant-runoff_voting>
- **Elections every three years**: (Elections) House terms last up to 3 years, among the shortest in the world. Senators serve 6 years, with half the Senate up at each election. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Australia>
- **Changing the Constitution is hard**: (Elections) It takes a referendum with a national majority plus a majority in at least four of the six states. Of 45 referendums, only 8 have passed. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Referendums_in_Australia>

### The economy in numbers

- **Size of the economy**: (Wealth · US$1.8 trillion) 2025 GDP, around the 15th biggest in the world, with only 28 million people.
- **GDP per person**: (Wealth · US$65,000) One of the 15 highest in the world (IMF, 2025).
- **Minimum wage**: (Work · A$26.44/hr) A$1,004.90 for a 38-hour week, since 1 July 2026.
- **Average weekly earnings**: (Work · A$2,084) Average for full-time adults (ABS, May 2026).
- **Unemployment**: (Work · 4.7%) In September 2026, a five-year high.
- **Weekly rent**: (Cost of living · A$700) Median advertised rent across the capitals in September 2026. In Sydney it’s over A$800.
- **Inflation**: (Cost of living · 4.0%) Over the 12 months to August 2026, above the Reserve Bank’s 2–3% target.
- **Cash rate**: (Cost of living · 4.60%) The Reserve Bank of Australia’s rate after its fourth rise of 2026, in September.
- **Superannuation**: (Work · 12%) Employers must pay 12% on top of wages into each worker’s retirement fund.

### Where the money comes from

- **Iron ore**: (Exports) The country’s biggest export: around A$121 billion in 2025, mostly from the Pilbara (WA) and mostly to China. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mining_in_Australia>
- **Coal**: (Exports) Around A$64 billion in 2025 and falling. The energy transition makes it one of the most fought-over topics in politics. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_in_Australia>
- **Natural gas**: (Exports) Around A$60 billion in 2025. Australia is one of the world’s biggest exporters of liquefied natural gas (LNG). <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_in_Australia>
- **Gold**: (Exports) Around A$60 billion in 2025, up 67% as prices soared. The gold rush never really ended. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mining_in_Australia>
- **International education**: (Services) Around A$55 billion in 2025: the biggest service the country sells to the world. International students keep whole suburbs humming. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_education>
- **Tourism**: (Services) Beaches, the Great Barrier Reef, Uluru and the cities draw millions of visitors a year. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Australia>
- **Health care and social assistance**: (Services) The country’s biggest employer, with hospitals, clinics, aged care and the NDIS (the disability scheme). <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_care_in_Australia>
- **Super funds**: (Services) Thanks to compulsory superannuation, retirement savings top A$4 trillion, one of the biggest pension pools in the world. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superannuation_in_Australia>
- **Grain, fruit and wine**: (Agriculture) Wheat, barley, canola, fruit and wine from regions like the Barossa and Margaret River are sold across Asia and the world. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agriculture_in_Australia>
- **China, the big partner**: (Trade) China is by far the biggest buyer of Australian goods, followed by Japan, South Korea, India and the US. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia%E2%80%93China_relations>
- **An expensive country**: (Cost of living) Rent, mortgages and groceries add up: a house in Sydney costs many times a family’s annual income. On the flip side, wages are among the highest in the world. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Australia>
- **Medicare and tax**: (Cost of living) Public health care is funded partly by a 2% levy on income. The goods and services tax (GST) is 10% and already included in the price. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicare_(Australia)>

### Billionaires and tycoons

- **Gina Rinehart**: (Mining) Owner of Hancock Prospecting, inherited from her father and multiplied on Pilbara iron ore. Usually the richest person in the country. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Rinehart>
- **Andrew “Twiggy” Forrest**: (Mining) Founder of Fortescue, the iron ore giant now betting on green energy. Gives away fortunes through the Minderoo Foundation. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Forrest>
- **Clive Palmer**: (Mining) Mining magnate who launched his own political party and promised to build a Titanic II. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Palmer>
- **Mike Cannon-Brookes and Scott Farquhar**: (Tech) The Atlassian founders who started out on a credit card. Cannon-Brookes has become one of the country’s biggest clean-energy investors. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Cannon-Brookes>
- **Melanie Perkins and Cliff Obrecht**: (Tech) The couple who created Canva and pledged to give away most of their stake in the company. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melanie_Perkins>
- **Rupert Murdoch**: (Media) Born in Melbourne, he built News Corp and Fox from a single Adelaide newspaper. Became a US citizen in 1985. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupert_Murdoch>
- **Kerry Packer**: (Media) Owner of Channel Nine who shook up cricket with World Series Cricket in 1977. He died in 2005. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerry_Packer>
- **James Packer**: (Media) Kerry Packer’s son, who bet big on casinos with Crown Resorts. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Packer>
- **Frank Lowy**: (Retail and property) A Holocaust survivor who co-founded Westfield in Sydney and took its shopping centres global. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Lowy>
- **Harry Triguboff**: (Retail and property) “High-rise Harry”, founder of Meriton, builder of thousands of apartments in Sydney and Brisbane. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Triguboff>
- **Gerry Harvey**: (Retail and property) Co-founder of Harvey Norman, the appliance and furniture chain. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerry_Harvey>
- **Anthony Pratt**: (Industry) Runs Visy, the packaging and cardboard recycling giant. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Pratt>
- **Lindsay Fox**: (Industry) Started with one truck and built Linfox, one of the biggest logistics companies in the Asia-Pacific. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindsay_Fox>

### The parties

- **Australian Labor Party**: (Major parties · 1891) Centre-left, born from the union movement. In government since 2022 under Anthony Albanese. Created Medicare and compulsory super. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Labor_Party>
- **Liberal Party**: (Major parties · 1944) Centre-right, founded by Robert Menzies. Leads the Opposition; since February 2026 its leader is Angus Taylor. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Party_of_Australia>
- **The Nationals**: (Major parties · 1920) The party of the bush and the farmers. Usually governs alongside the Liberals as the Coalition. Leader: Matt Canavan, since March 2026. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Party_of_Australia>
- **The Greens**: (Major parties · 1992) Climate, the environment and social justice. Strong in the Senate and the inner cities. Leader: Senator David Shoebridge, since September 2026. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Greens>
- **One Nation**: (Minor parties · 1997) Pauline Hanson’s right-wing populist party, critical of immigration. Holds seats in the Senate. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Nation>
- **The “teals”**: (Minor parties · 2022) Community independents, mostly women, campaigning on climate action and integrity in politics. They took traditionally Liberal seats in 2022. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teal_independents>
- **Katter’s Australian Party**: (Minor parties · 2011) Bob Katter’s party, focused on north Queensland and the bush. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katter%27s_Australian_Party>
- **Jacqui Lambie Network**: (Minor parties · 2015) Led by Tasmanian senator and ex-soldier Jacqui Lambie, known for speaking her mind. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacqui_Lambie_Network>

### Politicians

- **Anthony Albanese**: (Today) Prime Minister since 2022. Grew up in public housing in Sydney, raised by a single mum, and became the first PM with a non-Anglo-Celtic surname. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Albanese>
- **Jim Chalmers**: (Today) Treasurer in the Labor government, from Queensland. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Chalmers>
- **Penny Wong**: (Today) Foreign Minister, born in Malaysia. One of the country’s most respected politicians. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_Wong>
- **Angus Taylor**: (Today) Leader of the Liberal Party and the Opposition since February 2026, after toppling Sussan Ley in a spill. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angus_Taylor>
- **David Shoebridge**: (Today) New South Wales senator and former barrister, leader of the Greens since September 2026. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Shoebridge>
- **Matt Canavan**: (Today) Queensland senator and leader of the Nationals since March 2026, a champion of coal mining. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Canavan>
- **Pauline Hanson**: (Today) Founder of One Nation, a Queensland senator. A divisive figure in politics for almost 30 years. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pauline_Hanson>
- **David Pocock**: (Today) Former Wallabies captain turned independent senator for the ACT. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Pocock>
- **Lidia Thorpe**: (Today) Independent senator and Aboriginal activist, known for protesting at King Charles during his 2024 visit. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lidia_Thorpe>
- **Robert Menzies**: (Former PMs) The longest-serving PM, 18 years in all (1939–41 and 1949–66). Founded the Liberal Party. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Menzies>
- **Gough Whitlam**: (Former PMs) In just three years (1972–75) he brought in free university and Medibank, the forerunner of Medicare. Dismissed by the Governor-General. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gough_Whitlam>
- **Bob Hawke**: (Former PMs) PM from 1983 to 1991, created Medicare and opened up the economy. Hugely popular, he even held a beer-drinking record. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Hawke>
- **Paul Keating**: (Former PMs) PM from 1991 to 1996, famous for his sharp tongue and the Redfern speech (1992) on injustices against Aboriginal people. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Keating>
- **John Howard**: (Former PMs) PM from 1996 to 2007, the second-longest serving. Brought in the gun laws and the GST. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Howard>
- **Kevin Rudd**: (Former PMs) PM in 2007–10 and again in 2013. Delivered the Apology to the Stolen Generations in 2008. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Rudd>
- **Julia Gillard**: (Former PMs) The first woman to be prime minister (2010–13). Her 2012 “misogyny speech” went around the world. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia_Gillard>
- **Malcolm Turnbull**: (Former PMs) PM from 2015 to 2018, leading the government that legalised marriage equality after the 2017 postal survey. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcolm_Turnbull>
- **Scott Morrison**: (Former PMs) PM from 2018 to 2022, criticised for holidaying in Hawaii during the Black Summer bushfires. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Morrison>

### Activists

- **Eddie Mabo**: (Indigenous rights) A Torres Strait Islander who took his people’s fight for their land to the High Court. The 1992 decision ended the idea of “terra nullius”. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Mabo>
- **Vincent Lingiari**: (Indigenous rights) Led the Wave Hill walk-off (1966), when Gurindji workers walked off a cattle station. In 1975 Whitlam poured soil into his hand, returning part of their land. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Lingiari>
- **Charles Perkins**: (Indigenous rights) Led the 1965 Freedom Ride, a bus trip through country NSW exposing racial segregation. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Perkins_(Aboriginal_activist)>
- **Faith Bandler**: (Indigenous rights) One of the leading voices of the “yes” campaign in the 1967 referendum. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Bandler>
- **Megan Davis**: (Indigenous rights) Aboriginal legal scholar and one of the authors of the Uluru Statement from the Heart (2017), which called for an Indigenous Voice to Parliament. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Davis>
- **Thomas Mayo**: (Indigenous rights) Torres Strait Islander unionist who carried the Uluru Statement around the country during the 2023 campaign. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Mayo_(author)>
- **Adam Goodes**: (Indigenous rights) AFL champion and 2014 Australian of the Year who became a symbol of the fight against racism in sport. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Goodes>
- **Bob Brown**: (Climate and environment) Led the campaign that saved Tasmania’s Franklin River in 1983 and founded the Greens. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Brown>
- **Tim Flannery**: (Climate and environment) Scientist and author, one of the best-known voices on climate change. 2007 Australian of the Year. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Flannery>
- **Anjali Sharma**: (Climate and environment) At 16, led a group of students who took the government to court over the climate harm of a coal mine (2021). <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anjali_Sharma_(climate_activist)>
- **Vida Goldstein**: (Women) Melbourne suffragist who in 1903 was one of the first women in the British Empire to stand for a national parliament. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vida_Goldstein>
- **Edith Cowan**: (Women) The first woman elected to an Australian parliament, in Western Australia in 1921. She’s on the $50 note. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edith_Cowan>
- **Rosie Batty**: (Society) After losing her son to her former partner’s violence, she became the national voice against family violence. 2015 Australian of the Year. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosie_Batty>
- **Grace Tame**: (Society) A survivor of child sexual abuse who fought for the right to tell her story. 2021 Australian of the Year. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grace_Tame>
- **Dylan Alcott**: (Society) Paralympic tennis and basketball champion and disability rights advocate. 2022 Australian of the Year. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dylan_Alcott>
- **Taryn Brumfitt**: (Society) Founder of the Body Image Movement, pushing back against beauty pressure. 2023 Australian of the Year. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taryn_Brumfitt>
- **Peter Singer**: (Animal rights) Melbourne-born moral philosopher whose book Animal Liberation (1975) shaped the modern animal rights movement. Emeritus professor of bioethics at Princeton. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer>
- **Georgie Purcell**: (Animal rights) Animal Justice Party MP in Victoria’s upper house since 2022, campaigning for a ban on duck hunting and for animal welfare. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgie_Purcell>
- **Joey Carbstrong**: (Animal rights) Former criminal turned animal rights activist and vegan advocate, with undercover investigations and viral debates on social media. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joey_Carbstrong>

Sources: [AEC: how elections work](https://www.aec.gov.au); [Parliament of Australia](https://www.aph.gov.au); [ABS: earnings (May 2026) and unemployment (Sep 2026)](https://www.abs.gov.au); [RBA: cash rate](https://www.rba.gov.au); [Fair Work Ombudsman: minimum wage](https://www.fairwork.gov.au); [DFAT: 2025 exports](https://www.dfat.gov.au/trade/trade-and-investment-data-information-and-publications); [PropTrack/realestate.com.au: rents (Sep 2026)](https://www.realestate.com.au/insights/); [IMF: World Economic Outlook](https://www.imf.org/en/Publications/WEO)

## Find out more

https://australianculture.biblioverse.org/websites.html

- **Australia.com**: (Tourism and image · Tourism Australia) The official tourism site: destinations, itineraries, events and the Aussie way of life explained for visitors. <https://www.australia.com>
- **Australia’s Nation Brand**: (Tourism and image · Australian Government) How Australia presents itself to the world, with the kangaroo logo, colours, photos and stories to use. <https://www.brandaustralia.com>
- **Study Australia**: (Tourism and image · Austrade) The official portal for international students: courses, cost of living and what it’s like to live here. <https://www.studyaustralia.gov.au>
- **DFAT: About Australia**: (Tourism and image · Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade) An official overview of the country: people, government, economy, culture and the “Australia in Brief” booklet. <https://www.dfat.gov.au/about-australia>
- **Digital Atlas of Australia**: (Data and maps · Geoscience Australia) The government’s interactive atlas: layer up maps of population, climate, land, infrastructure and much more. <https://digital.atlas.gov.au>
- **ABS**: (Data and maps · Australian Bureau of Statistics) The national statistics agency: the Census, population, the economy and “Data by Region” to compare any town. <https://www.abs.gov.au>
- **Geoscience Australia**: (Data and maps · Australian Government) Geology, earthquakes, official maps and trivia like the continent’s extreme points. <https://www.ga.gov.au>
- **Bureau of Meteorology**: (Data and maps · BOM) Forecasts, radar, climate averages for every town and the UV index that every Aussie checks. <https://www.bom.gov.au>
- **AIATSIS**: (First Peoples · Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies) The leading research centre and collection on First Peoples, home of the well-known map of Indigenous Australia. <https://aiatsis.gov.au>
- **First Languages Australia**: (First Peoples · Indigenous organisation) Works to keep Indigenous languages alive. Its Gambay map brings together hundreds of languages and dialects. <https://www.firstlanguages.org.au>
- **Reconciliation Australia**: (First Peoples · Independent organisation) Explains reconciliation between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australians, Acknowledgement of Country and the key dates. <https://www.reconciliation.org.au>
- **Indigenous.gov.au**: (First Peoples · National Indigenous Australians Agency) News, programs and stories from Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities. <https://www.indigenous.gov.au>
- **National Archives of Australia**: (Culture and history · National Archives) Records that tell the country’s story, from Federation to migrant arrivals. <https://www.naa.gov.au>
- **Trove**: (Culture and history · National Library of Australia) Millions of digitised old newspapers, photos, books and maps. You can read the news from 1803 onwards. <https://trove.nla.gov.au>
- **National Museum of Australia**: (Culture and history · National Museum) The museum of the country’s history and culture, in Canberra, with collections and exhibitions online. <https://www.nma.gov.au>
- **Australian War Memorial**: (Culture and history · War memorial) For understanding Anzac Day and the weight of war in the national identity. <https://www.awm.gov.au>
- **Australian Museum**: (Culture and history · The country’s oldest museum) Founded in Sydney in 1827. Great for getting to know the wildlife (dangerous ones included) and Indigenous cultures. <https://australian.museum>
- **Screen Australia**: (Culture and history · Screen agency) Data and catalogues of Australian films, series and animation. <https://www.screenaustralia.gov.au>
- **ABC**: (Media · Public broadcaster) Aunty: news, radio, podcasts and ABC iview, home of shows like Bluey. <https://www.abc.net.au>
- **SBS**: (Media · Multicultural public broadcaster) The broadcaster for migrant communities, with content in dozens of languages, including SBS Portuguese. <https://www.sbs.com.au>
- **Parks Australia**: (Nature · National parks) Uluru-Kata Tjuta, Kakadu, Booderee and the other Commonwealth parks, with visitor tips and local culture. <https://parksaustralia.gov.au>
- **Atlas of Living Australia**: (Nature · CSIRO and partners) Millions of records of plants and animals. Find out what lives near any address. <https://www.ala.org.au>

## Are you true blue?

https://australianculture.biblioverse.org/quiz.html

- **What is Vegemite?**: Answer: A yeast-extract spread
- **What’s the capital of Australia?**: Answer: Canberra
- **Which invention came out of a CSIRO lab?**: Answer: Fast Wi-Fi
- **When an Aussie talks about “thongs”, they mean...**: Answer: Flip-flops
- **Who won the Great Emu War of 1932?**: Answer: The emus
- **Which Australian actor starred in Barbie (2023)?**: Answer: Margot Robbie
- **What is Australia’s national floral emblem?**: Answer: Golden wattle
- **Which of these mammals lays eggs?**: Answer: Platypus
- **Which is the longest fence in the world, at 5,614 km?**: Answer: Dingo Fence
- **Which band recorded “Down Under”?**: Answer: Men at Work
- **When is Anzac Day?**: Answer: 25 April
- **Which animal makes cube-shaped poo?**: Answer: Wombat
- **Which Aussie bird has a call that sounds like laughter?**: Answer: Kookaburra
- **What does it mean to “shout” at the pub?**: Answer: Buy a round
- **Which dog breed is Bluey?**: Answer: Blue heeler
